title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README. It also uses fastapi, which no GeoLattice option installs: pip install fastapi.


Code
# Imports, AOI parameters, and Planetary Computer client for the capstone
%matplotlib inline
import difflib

import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles

from IPython.display import IFrame, display

import geolattice

from geolattice.vector import write_geoparquet, read_geoparquet

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})
DATA = Path("../../../Data")
BD = DATA / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "Bangladesh"
WEB = DATA / "00_shared" / "data_web_cloud_gis"
OUT = WEB / "08_11_outputs"

(OUT / "water").mkdir(parents=True)

AOI = (90.95, 24.95, 91.25, 25.20)          # ~30 x 28 km: Tanguar Haor, Sunamganj town and surrounding haors

YEAR = 2024
TRACK = 41                                     # Sentinel-1 relative orbit (ascending): one viewing geometry
THRESHOLD_DB = -20.0                           # VH backscatter below this is open water (Section 4)
VV_THRESHOLD_DB = -18.0                        # the common VV rule, kept for comparison
pcc = pystac_client.Client.open("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1", modifier=planetary_computer.sign_inplace)
print("geolattice", geolattice.__version__, "| outputs:", OUT)

title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
text:
Architecture
 Planetary Computer (STAC + COGs)            Processing (this notebook / a scheduled container)
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐   search    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ sentinel-1-rtc  jrc-gsw     │ ──────────► │ odc-stac load → dB → water mask (VH < −20 dB)│
 └─────────────────────────────┘   read      │ per-union statistics, flood frequency        │
                                             └───────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                                             │ write (idempotent)
                        Storage (object storage in production)▼
                ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                │ water/*.tif (COG) · flood_frequency.tif (COG)                │
                │ unions_flood.parquet (GeoParquet) · union_series.parquet     │
                │ stac/catalog.json (STAC)                                     │
                └───────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
                                │                               │
          Service (FastAPI + geolattice.web)                  Any STAC / GIS client
   /ogc  tiles + OGC API Features (geolattice.web.create_app)   (QGIS, GDAL, STAC Browser)
   /api  dates, union time series, rankings
   /map  web map (Leaflet) calling /ogc and /api
Processing writes files; the service only reads them. Each part can be replaced or scaled without touching the others: the files can move to S3 or Azure Blob, the service can run in several containers behind a load balancer, and the processing can run on a schedule (Notebook 08_10).

title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
text:
Data: Sentinel-1 over the haors
Radar sees through cloud, so it observes the haors throughout the monsoon, when Sentinel-2 saw nothing usable (Notebook 08_10). Open water reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite and appears dark. We use the RTC product (backscatter normalised for terrain) and a single relative orbit, so that every acquisition has the same viewing geometry and the time series is comparable.


Code
# Search Sentinel-1 RTC for the year and summarize orbits and revisit gaps
t0 = time.perf_counter()
items = list(pcc.search(collections=["sentinel-1-rtc"], bbox=list(AOI), datetime=f"{YEAR}-01-01/{YEAR}-12-31").items())
tracks = pd.DataFrame([{"track": i.properties["sat:relative_orbit"], "direction": i.properties["sat:orbit_state"],
                        "platform": i.properties["platform"], "date": i.datetime.date()} for i in items])
print(f"{len(items)} Sentinel-1 RTC items over the area in {YEAR} ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
display(tracks.groupby(["track", "direction", "platform"]).date.agg(["count", "nunique", "min", "max"])
        .rename(columns={"count": "items", "nunique": "dates"}))
# Keep only the chosen relative orbit so geometry stays consistent
by_day = {}
for i in items:
    if i.properties["sat:relative_orbit"] == TRACK:
        by_day.setdefault(i.datetime.date(), []).append(i)
dates = sorted(by_day)
gaps = np.diff(pd.to_datetime(dates)).astype("timedelta64[D]").astype(int)
print(f"track {TRACK}: {len(dates)} dates, gaps between acquisitions: {sorted(set(gaps))} days")

title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
section: Water from radar: choosing the band and the threshold
text:
Water from radar: choosing the band and the threshold
Calm open water reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite, so it is dark in both polarisations: co-polarised VV and cross-polarised VH. Wind and waves roughen the water surface and brighten VV much more than VH. The haors are large, shallow and windy in the monsoon, so we compare both bands on a dry-season and a flood-season date before choosing.


Code
# Load VV/VH in dB for dry and flood-season dates; compare water thresholds
def load_db(day):
    "VV and VH backscatter in dB for one acquisition date on the 30 m AOI grid (average resampling reduces speckle)."
    ds = odc.stac.load(by_day[day], bands=["vv", "vh"], bbox=list(AOI), crs=CRS, resolution=RES, groupby="solar_day",
                       resampling="average").isel(time=0)
    out = {}
    for band in ["vv", "vh"]:
        v = ds[band].values.astype("float32")
        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            out[band] = np.where(v > 0, 10 * np.log10(v), np.nan)
    return out, ds.odc.geobox

dry = min(dates, key=lambda d: abs((pd.Timestamp(d) - pd.Timestamp(f"{YEAR}-02-15")).days))
wet = min(dates, key=lambda d: abs((pd.Timestamp(d) - pd.Timestamp(f"{YEAR}-10-03")).days))
db_dry, geobox = load_db(dry)
db_wet, _ = load_db(wet)
# Histograms and grayscale maps, then a small threshold sensitivity table
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 4.2))
for a, band, thr in [(ax[0], "vv", VV_THRESHOLD_DB), (ax[1], "vh", THRESHOLD_DB)]:
    bins = np.linspace(-32, 2, 120)
    a.hist(db_dry[band][np.isfinite(db_dry[band])], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, label=f"dry {dry}")
    a.hist(db_wet[band][np.isfinite(db_wet[band])], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, label=f"flood season {wet}")
    a.axvline(thr, color="k", ls="--"); a.set_title(f"{band.upper()} backscatter (dB), threshold {thr:g}"); a.legend(fontsize=8)
for a, band in [(ax[2], "vv"), (ax[3], "vh")]:
    a.imshow(db_wet[band], cmap="gray", vmin=-28 if band == "vh" else -25, vmax=-8 if band == "vh" else 0)
    a.set_title(f"{band.upper()}, {wet}"); a.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
sens = pd.DataFrame({
    **{f"VV < {t}": [np.nanmean(db_dry["vv"] < t), np.nanmean(db_wet["vv"] < t)] for t in [-20, -18, -16]},
    **{f"VH < {t}": [np.nanmean(db_dry["vh"] < t), np.nanmean(db_wet["vh"] < t)] for t in [-22, -21, -20, -19, -18]}},
    index=[f"dry {dry}", f"flood season {wet}"])
print("share of the area classified as water (%):")
(sens * 100).round(1)

On 3 October the haors were full, yet VV classified only 0.6% of the area as water: the images show the open water grey and textured in VV, roughened by wind, and uniformly dark in VH. VH separates the two seasons cleanly. Its water mode sits near −22 dB, close to the sensor’s noise floor, and its land mode is around −15 dB. A threshold of −20 dB lies between them; moving it by ±1 dB changes the flood-season estimate by about 4-10 points.

title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
text:
Processing 2024: water maps every 12 days
For each acquisition the processing step loads VV and VH, classifies water from VH, and writes a small Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF (1 = water, 0 = land, 255 = no data), plus a JSON sidecar with the area’s water share under both rules. It skips dates whose COG already exists, so rerunning it, or running it on a schedule, only processes new acquisitions.


Code
# Write an idempotent water-mask COG for every acquisition date
def water_path(day):
    return OUT / "water" / f"water_{day}.tif"

def process_day(day):
    "Water mask for one date as a COG; skipped if it exists (idempotent)."
    path = water_path(day)
    if path.exists():
        return "skipped"
    db, gb = load_db(day)
    ok = np.isfinite(db["vh"])
    mask = np.where(ok, (db["vh"] < THRESHOLD_DB).astype("uint8"), 255).astype("uint8")
    path.with_suffix(".json").write_text(json.dumps({
        "valid_pct": float(ok.mean() * 100), "vh_water_pct": float(np.nanmean(db["vh"][ok] < THRESHOLD_DB) * 100),
        "vv_water_pct": float(np.nanmean(db["vv"][np.isfinite(db["vv"])] < VV_THRESHOLD_DB) * 100),
        "median_vv_db": float(np.nanmedian(db["vv"])), "median_vh_db": float(np.nanmedian(db["vh"]))}))
    tmp = path.with_suffix(".tmp.tif")
    with rasterio.open(tmp, "w", driver="GTiff", width=mask.shape[1], height=mask.shape[0], count=1, dtype="uint8",
                       crs=CRS, transform=gb.affine, nodata=255) as dst:
        dst.write(mask, 1)
    web.to_cog(tmp, path, compress="DEFLATE", overview_resampling="NEAREST")
    tmp.unlink()
    return "processed"

# First pass processes; second pass should skip existing COGs
t0 = time.perf_counter()
status = {d: process_day(d) for d in dates}
first_run = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
status_again = {d: process_day(d) for d in dates}
second_run = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"first run: {list(status.values()).count('processed')} dates processed in {first_run:.0f} s; "
      f"second run: {list(status_again.values()).count('skipped')} skipped in {second_run:.2f} s")
cogs = sorted((OUT / "water").glob("*.tif"))
print(f"{len(cogs)} COGs, {sum(p.stat().st_size for p in cogs) / 1e6:.1f} MB in total;", web.validate_cog(cogs[0]))
rules = pd.DataFrame([json.loads(water_path(d).with_suffix(".json").read_text()) for d in dates], index=pd.to_datetime(dates))
monsoon = rules.loc[f"{YEAR}-06-01":f"{YEAR}-10-31"]
print("monsoon (June-October) water share, % of area:")
display(pd.DataFrame({rule: {"min": monsoon[c].min(), "max": monsoon[c].max(),
                             "mean absolute change between acquisitions": monsoon[c].diff().abs().mean()}
                      for rule, c in [(f"VV < {VV_THRESHOLD_DB:g} dB", "vv_water_pct"), (f"VH < {THRESHOLD_DB:g} dB", "vh_water_pct")]}).T.round(1))
print(f"median VV over the area ranged from {monsoon.median_vv_db.min():.1f} to {monsoon.median_vv_db.max():.1f} dB in the monsoon; "
      f"median VH from {monsoon.median_vh_db.min():.1f} to {monsoon.median_vh_db.max():.1f} dB")

title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
section: Flood frequency and statistics per union
text:
Flood frequency and statistics per union
The water maps are stacked to give, for every pixel, the share of 2024 acquisitions in which it was water (flood frequency). For administrative statistics each union is rasterised once onto the same grid; the water share of every union on every date is then a fast count.


Code
# Stack water masks into flood frequency and zonal stats by union
with rasterio.open(cogs[0]) as src:
    transform, shape = src.transform, src.shape
stack = np.stack([rasterio.open(p).read(1) for p in cogs])            # (dates, rows, cols)
valid = stack != 255
water = (stack == 1)
frequency = np.where(valid.any(0), water.sum(0) / np.maximum(valid.sum(0), 1) * 100, np.nan).astype("float32")
with rasterio.open(OUT / "flood_frequency.tmp.tif", "w", driver="GTiff", width=shape[1], height=shape[0], count=1,
                   dtype="float32", crs=CRS, transform=transform, nodata=np.nan) as dst:
    dst.write(frequency, 1)
web.to_cog(OUT / "flood_frequency.tmp.tif", OUT / "flood_frequency.tif"); (OUT / "flood_frequency.tmp.tif").unlink()

# Rasterize Bangladesh unions and compute water % per union and date
unions = gpd.read_file(BD / "Shapefiles" / "bd_union_GCS.shp")[["ADM4_EN", "ADM4_PCODE", "ADM3_EN", "ADM2_EN", "geometry"]]
unions = unions[unions.intersects(shapely.box(*AOI))].reset_index(drop=True)
zones = rasterize([(g, i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(unions.to_crs(CRS).geometry)], out_shape=shape, transform=transform, fill=0)
box_utm = gpd.GeoSeries([shapely.box(*AOI)], crs=4326).to_crs(CRS).iloc[0]
cover = (unions.to_crs(CRS).intersection(box_utm).area / unions.to_crs(CRS).area).values      # share of each union inside the AOI
rows = []
for k, day in enumerate(dates):
    w = np.bincount(zones.ravel(), weights=water[k].ravel(), minlength=len(unions) + 1)[1:]
    v = np.bincount(zones.ravel(), weights=valid[k].ravel(), minlength=len(unions) + 1)[1:]
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({"ADM4_PCODE": unions.ADM4_PCODE, "date": pd.Timestamp(day),
                              "water_pct": np.where(v > 0, w / np.maximum(v, 1) * 100, np.nan)}))
series = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
series["month"] = series.date.dt.month
summary = series.groupby("ADM4_PCODE").agg(water_min=("water_pct", "min"), water_max=("water_pct", "max"),
                                            water_mean=("water_pct", "mean"))
summary["months_over_50pct"] = series[series.water_pct > 50].groupby("ADM4_PCODE").month.nunique().reindex(summary.index).fillna(0).astype(int)
peak = series.loc[series.groupby("ADM4_PCODE").water_pct.idxmax(), ["ADM4_PCODE", "date"]].set_index("ADM4_PCODE").date
summary["peak_date"] = peak.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
unions = unions.merge(summary.round(1), left_on="ADM4_PCODE", right_index=True)
unions["inside_aoi_pct"] = (cover * 100).round(0)
area = series.groupby("date").water_pct.median()
aoi_water = pd.Series([water[k][valid[k]].mean() * 100 for k in range(len(dates))], index=pd.to_datetime(dates), name="AOI water %")
print(f"{len(unions)} unions intersect the area; {len(dates)} dates; series table {len(series):,} rows")
print(f"area-wide water: minimum {aoi_water.min():.1f} % ({aoi_water.idxmin().date()}), maximum {aoi_water.max():.1f} % ({aoi_water.idxmax().date()})")
display(unions.drop(columns="geometry").sort_values("water_mean", ascending=False).head(8))

ax3.legend(fontsize=8)

Processing the 29 dates took 294 s, network reads included. The rerun skipped every date in no time, which is the property a scheduled job needs. The 29 water maps total 2.0 MB as COGs.

The VV jumps are not floods coming and going every 12 days. They follow the wind, which raised the area’s median VV by up to 9 dB on some dates while median VH stayed within about 1 dB.
The year in the haors (VH):

January: water drained from 28% of the area to 8% by early February.
Dry season: 4.5-8% from February to April, mostly permanent beels and rivers.
Rise: about 11% through May, then a jump to 66% by 5 June and a peak of 78.2% on 17 June, consistent with the early-monsoon floods reported in Sylhet division that month.
Monsoon: 57-77% until mid-October.
Recession: from 65% at the end of October to 34% by late December.

Unions: the 28 unions that intersect the area differ widely. Dakshin Sreepur, Tahirpur and Beheli, which lie entirely inside the area, were more than half under water in 7-8 months, with mean water shares of 55-61%. Some unions only touch the area (as little as 2% of their area inside), and their statistics describe only that part; the table’s inside_aoi_pct column says so.

title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
text:
Validation
Two independent checks:

Sentinel-2. Notebook 08_10’s monitor recorded the open-water fraction of Tanguar Haor (a sub-area of this AOI) from optical images. Where a Sentinel-2 observation lies within 3 days of a Sentinel-1 acquisition, the two estimates are compared for the same sub-area.
JRC Global Surface Water (1984-2020). Pixels that were water in most years’ records should be water in this year’s flood season, and dry-season water should fall on permanent water bodies.



Code
# Compare Sentinel-1 water over Tanguar Haor with optical results from Notebook 08_10
TANGUAR = (91.02, 25.08, 91.14, 25.17)
from rasterio.windows import from_bounds
from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds
win = from_bounds(*transform_bounds(4326, CRS, *TANGUAR), transform)
r0, c0 = int(win.row_off), int(win.col_off)
r1, c1 = r0 + int(win.height), c0 + int(win.width)
s1_tanguar = pd.Series([water[k, r0:r1, c0:c1][valid[k, r0:r1, c0:c1]].mean() for k in range(len(dates))],
                       index=pd.to_datetime(dates), name="Sentinel-1")
s2_path = WEB / "08_10_outputs" / "monitor_data" / "observations.parquet"
if s2_path.exists():
    s2 = pd.read_parquet(s2_path)

    pairs = []

        k = int(np.argmin(np.abs(s1_tanguar.index - d)))
        if abs((s1_tanguar.index[k] - d).days) <= 3:
            pairs.append({"Sentinel-2 date": d.date(), "Sentinel-1 date": s1_tanguar.index[k].date(),
                          "Sentinel-2 water": v, "Sentinel-1 water": s1_tanguar.iloc[k]})
    pairs = pd.DataFrame(pairs)
    assert len(pairs) >= 3, "too few matching dates for a comparison"
    r = np.corrcoef(pairs["Sentinel-2 water"], pairs["Sentinel-1 water"])[0, 1]
    bias = (pairs["Sentinel-1 water"] - pairs["Sentinel-2 water"]).mean()
    display(pairs.round(3))
    print(f"{len(pairs)} pairs within 3 days: correlation {r:.2f}, mean difference (S1 - S2) {bias:+.3f}")

title: Capstone: A Cloud Web-GIS for Flood Monitoring in the Haor Basin
text:
Summary: from data to decisions
The capstone joined the module’s parts into one working system for the Sunamganj haors in 2024:

Data: 29 Sentinel-1 RTC acquisitions found through STAC and read lazily with odc-stac (08_09).
Method: a water rule chosen by evidence. VH < −20 dB was stable through the monsoon, while the common VV rule swung between 0.1% and 61.5% with the wind.
Results:

water rose from 4.5% of the area in March to 78.2% on 17 June;
it stayed above 57% until October and receded to 34% by December;
three fully covered unions were more than half under water in 7-8 months.

Validation: correlation 0.98 with Sentinel-2 (08_10), and agreement with 37 years of JRC water records. The known bias is about 6% false water on dry land in the dry season.
Products: COGs, GeoParquet and a validated STAC catalogue (08_01, 08_02), 4.3 MB in total.
Service: FastAPI with geolattice.web tiles and OGC API: Features (08_05, 08_06), and a web map calling the API (08_04, 08_07).
Operations: idempotent processing and seven passing service tests (08_10).

What the system adds beyond a map. Officers can see which unions flood first and longest, and when; researchers can pull the union series as GeoParquet or through OGC API: Features into their own tools; any STAC client can find the water maps by place and date; and the whole chain reruns itself as new radar images arrive.
Limitations to state with the results.

A single threshold misses water under vegetation (flooded rice and reeds can scatter strongly) and can mistake smooth dry surfaces and radar shadow for water.
VH water sits close to the sensor’s noise floor; the threshold (−20 dB) is tuned to this area and season and should be re-checked elsewhere.
Wind roughens open water. It made the common VV rule unusable here; VH is far less affected but not immune.
30 m pixels blur narrow channels.
Union statistics are only as good as the boundaries.

Exercises

Replace the fixed VH threshold by an automatic one per date (Otsu’s method on the dB histogram) and compare the water series and the validation of Section 7.
Add the descending track (relative orbit 150) to double the time resolution. What must you check before mixing tracks?
Detect early flash floods: unions whose water share rises by more than 20 points between two acquisitions in March-May, when Boro rice is still in the field. Add an /api/alerts endpoint.
Add Sentinel-2 NDVI of the cropland (Notebook 08_10’s monitor) to the union popups.
Package the processing as a haor_monitor-style project with tests, a Dockerfile and a schedule, and the service as a second image; write a compose.yaml that runs both.

References

Twele, A., Cao, W., Plank, S. & Martinis, S. (2016). Sentinel-1-based flood mapping: a fully automated processing chain. International Journal of Remote Sensing, 37(13), 2990-3004.
Uddin, K., Matin, M. A. & Meyer, F. J. (2019). Operational flood mapping using multi-temporal Sentinel-1 SAR images: a case study from Bangladesh. Remote Sensing, 11(13), 1581.
Pekel, J.-F. et al. (2016). High-resolution mapping of global surface water and its long-term changes. Nature, 540, 418-422.
Microsoft Planetary Computer: Sentinel-1 RTC. https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/dataset/sentinel-1-rtc
STAC specification. https://stacspec.org

section: Same scene, different numbers: the Sentinel-2 offset
text:
Same scene, different numbers: the Sentinel-2 offset
Since processing baseline 04.00 (January 2022), ESA stores Sentinel-2 L2A reflectance with an offset: reflectance = (DN − 1000) / 10000, so that dark pixels are not clipped at zero. Providers handle this differently. We read the same 12 × 11 km window of the red and near-infrared bands of the same scene (9 March 2024) from Planetary Computer and Earth Search.


Code
# Pick the latest date present in both Planetary Computer and Earth Search

es_items = {i.datetime.date(): i for i in found["Earth Search (AWS)"]}
day = sorted(set(pc_items) & set(es_items))[-1]
pc_item, es_item = pc_items[day], es_items[day]

# Window-read one band over the AOI without downloading the full COG
def window(href):
    with rasterio.Env(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN="EMPTY_DIR", AWS_NO_SIGN_REQUEST="YES"):
        with rasterio.open(href) as src:
            return src.read(1, window=from_bounds(*transform_bounds(4326, src.crs, *AOI), src.transform)).astype("float64")

bands = {"PC red": window(pc_item.assets["B04"].href), "PC nir": window(pc_item.assets["B08"].href),
         "ES red": window(es_item.assets["red"].href), "ES nir": window(es_item.assets["nir"].href)}
# Compare digital numbers where both catalogues have valid pixels
valid = np.all([b > 0 for b in bands.values()], axis=0)
diff = bands["PC red"][valid] - bands["ES red"][valid]
print(f"scene {day}: PC {pc_item.id} | ES {es_item.id}")
print(f"processing baseline: PC {pc_item.properties.get('s2:processing_baseline')}, ES {es_item.properties.get('s2:processing_baseline')}; "
      f"ES 'earthsearch:boa_offset_applied' = {es_item.properties.get('earthsearch:boa_offset_applied')}")
print(f"PC red minus ES red: median {np.median(diff):.0f}, range {diff.min():.0f} to {diff.max():.0f} (DN), {valid.sum():,} pixels")
print("ES metadata for the red band:", es_item.assets["red"].extra_fields.get("raster:bands"))

Code
# NDVI from the same pixels under correct and incorrect reflectance recipes
def ndvi(red, nir):
    return (nir - red) / (nir + red)

recipes = {
    "PC, DN used as is (wrong)": ndvi(bands["PC red"], bands["PC nir"]),
    "PC, (DN - 1000) / 10000 (correct)": ndvi(bands["PC red"] - 1000, bands["PC nir"] - 1000),
    "ES, DN / 10000 (correct: offset already applied)": ndvi(bands["ES red"], bands["ES nir"]),
    "ES, metadata scale and offset applied (wrong: offset twice)": ndvi(bands["ES red"] * 1e-4 - 0.1, bands["ES nir"] * 1e-4 - 0.1),
}
# Score each recipe against the correct Earth Search scaling
reference = recipes["ES, DN / 10000 (correct: offset already applied)"][valid]
rows = []
for name, v in recipes.items():
    v = v[valid]
    ok = np.isfinite(v) & (np.abs(v) <= 1)
    rows.append({"recipe": name, "median NDVI": np.median(v[ok]), "median abs. difference from correct": np.median(np.abs(v - reference)),
                 "impossible values (|NDVI| > 1 or infinite)": 1 - ok.mean(), "share of pixels NDVI > 0.5": (v[ok] > 0.5).mean()})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("recipe").round(3)

The two copies of the same scene, at the same processing baseline (05.10), differ by a median of exactly 1,000 DN:

Planetary Computer delivers ESA’s original values, with the offset still in them.
Earth Search has subtracted it (boa_offset_applied: true), yet its STAC metadata still advertises offset: -0.1.

Individual pixels differ by 800 to 1,288, so the two copies are not bit-identical apart from the offset either.

Using Planetary Computer’s DN as is understates NDVI by 0.18. With the offset subtracted twice, 77% of pixels get impossible NDVI values (beyond ±1 or infinite).
The rule: read s2:processing_baseline and the provider’s offset convention, and test one scene from each source before mixing them.

title: Cloud Platforms: Planetary Computer, Earth Engine and Copernicus openEO
section: Compute next to the catalogue: a cloud-free composite with odc-stac
text:
Compute next to the catalogue: a cloud-free composite with odc-stac
odc.stac.load turns a list of STAC items into an xarray Dataset on a common grid, lazily with Dask: only the requested bands and only the area of interest are read. We load all Planetary Computer scenes of the season with up to 20 % cloud, mask clouds, shadows and water with the scene classification layer (SCL), apply the offset, and take the per-pixel median NDVI.


Code
# Lazy-load a multi-date Sentinel-2 cube over the AOI with odc-stac
pcc = pystac_client.Client.open("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1", modifier=planetary_computer.sign_inplace)
items = list(pcc.search(collections=["sentinel-2-l2a"], bbox=AOI, datetime=SEASON, query={"eo:cloud_cover": {"lt": 20}}).items())
t0 = time.perf_counter()
cube = odc.stac.load(items, bands=["B02", "B03", "B04", "B08", "SCL"], bbox=AOI, resolution=10, crs="EPSG:32645",
                     chunks={}, groupby="solar_day", dtype="uint16")
print(f"{len(items)} items -> {cube.sizes['time']} dates, {cube.sizes['y']} x {cube.sizes['x']} pixels; "
      f"lazy dataset of {cube.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB defined in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
cube = cube.compute()
print(f"read in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

# Mask to clear land, convert DN to reflectance, then build a median NDVI composite
clear = cube.SCL.isin([4, 5])                                     # SCL 4 vegetation, 5 bare soil
refl = {b: ((cube[b].astype("float32") - 1000) / 1e4).where(clear) for b in ["B02", "B03", "B04", "B08"]}
nd = (refl["B08"] - refl["B04"]) / (refl["B08"] + refl["B04"])
composite = nd.median("time")
n_clear = clear.sum("time")
scl_share = pd.Series(cube.SCL.values.ravel()).map({0: "no data", 1: "saturated", 2: "dark", 3: "cloud shadow", 4: "vegetation",
                                                     5: "bare soil", 6: "water", 7: "unclassified", 8: "cloud (medium)",
                                                     9: "cloud (high)", 10: "thin cirrus", 11: "snow"}).value_counts(normalize=True)
print("scene classification over all dates:", (scl_share * 100).round(1).head(6).to_dict())
print(f"clear observations per pixel: median {int(n_clear.median())}, min {int(n_clear.min())}; median composite NDVI {float(composite.median()):.3f}")


10 items -> 9 dates, 1129 x 1233 pixels; lazy dataset of 125 MB defined in 0.02 s
read in 18.5 s
scene classification over all dates: {'bare soil': 79.4, 'vegetation': 16.2, 'unclassified': 2.5, 'cloud (medium)': 0.6, 'water': 0.5, 'thin cirrus': 0.4}
clear observations per pixel: median 9, min 0; median composite NDVI 0.449




Code
# Plot true colour, median NDVI, and the area NDVI time series
best = int(clear.mean(("x", "y")).argmax())
rgb = np.stack([(cube[b].isel(time=best).astype("float32") - 1000) / 1e4 for b in ["B04", "B03", "B02"]], axis=-1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.6))
ax[0].imshow(np.clip(rgb / 0.25, 0, 1)); ax[0].set_title(f"True colour, {str(cube.time.values[best])[:10]}")
im = ax[1].imshow(composite, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=0.9); ax[1].set_title("Median NDVI, clear pixels, Jan-Mar 2024")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8)
monthly = nd.median(("x", "y")).to_series()
ax[2].plot(monthly.index, monthly.values, "o-"); ax[2].set_title("Median NDVI of the area by date"); ax[2].set_ylim(0, 0.8)
ax[2].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30)
for a in ax[:2]:
    a.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# Write GeoTIFF then convert and validate a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF
composite.rio.write_crs("EPSG:32645").rio.to_raster(OUT / "bogra_ndvi_median_2024q1.tif", compress="deflate")
print(web.validate_cog(web.to_cog(OUT / "bogra_ndvi_median_2024q1.tif", OUT / "bogra_ndvi_median_2024q1_cog.tif")))









../../../data/data_web_cloud_gis/08_09_outputs/bogra_ndvi_median_2024q1_cog.tif: valid Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF


odc-stac defined a 125 MB lazy dataset (9 dates, 1,129 × 1,233 pixels at 10 m) in 0.02 s and read it from Azure in 18.5 s. The scene classification shows the dry season: 79.4% of observations are classed bare soil, which includes freshly transplanted and irrigated Boro fields, and 16.2% vegetation. Clouds were rare, so every pixel had a median of 9 clear observations.
The median composite (NDVI 0.449) separates Bogra town and the main roads (red) from the surrounding fields and village groves (green). The date series dips on 18 January, probably from winter haze. The composite was saved as a GeoTIFF and converted with geolattice.web.to_cog into a valid COG, ready for the tile server of Notebook 08_05.

title: Cloud Platforms: Planetary Computer, Earth Engine and Copernicus openEO
section: Beyond imagery: ready-made global layers for a haor district
text:
Beyond imagery: ready-made global layers for a haor district
Planetary Computer also hosts analysis-ready global products. For Sunamganj district, in the haor basin of the north-east, we load three of them at 30 m: ESA WorldCover 2021 (land cover), Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (elevation) and JRC Global Surface Water occurrence (the share of 1984-2020 Landsat observations in which each pixel was water).


Code
# Load Sunamganj districts and pull three global layers from Planetary Computer
districts = gpd.read_file(WEB / "08_03_outputs" / "districts.gpkg")
sun = districts[districts.district == "Sunamganj"]
bbox = list(sun.total_bounds)
layers = {"esa-worldcover": ("map", "nearest"), "cop-dem-glo-30": ("data", "bilinear"), "jrc-gsw": ("occurrence", "nearest")}
grids, rows = {}, []
for collection, (asset, resampling) in layers.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    its = list(pcc.search(collections=[collection], bbox=bbox).items())
    if collection == "esa-worldcover":
        its = [i for i in its if "2021" in i.id]
    ds = odc.stac.load(its, bands=[asset], bbox=bbox, resolution=30, crs="EPSG:32646", resampling=resampling,
                       chunks={}).isel(time=0)
    grid = ds[asset].compute()
    grids[collection] = grid
    rows.append({"layer": collection, "items": len(its), "grid": f"{grid.sizes['y']} x {grid.sizes['x']}", "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1)})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("layer"))

# Restrict raster stats to the district polygon
from rasterio.features import geometry_mask
g0 = grids["esa-worldcover"]
inside = geometry_mask([sun.to_crs(32646).geometry.iloc[0]], out_shape=g0.shape, transform=g0.odc.geobox.affine, invert=True)
classes = {10: "Tree cover", 20: "Shrubland", 30: "Grassland", 40: "Cropland", 50: "Built-up", 60: "Bare / sparse",
           70: "Snow and ice", 80: "Permanent water", 90: "Herbaceous wetland", 95: "Mangroves", 100: "Moss and lichen"}
lc = pd.Series(g0.values[inside]).map(classes).value_counts(normalize=True).mul(100).round(1)
dem = grids["cop-dem-glo-30"].values[inside]
occ_grid = grids["jrc-gsw"].values.astype(float)
occ_grid[occ_grid > 100] = np.nan                                   # 255 = no data
occ = occ_grid[inside]
print(f"Sunamganj district: {inside.sum() * 900 / 1e6:,.0f} km² at 30 m")
print("land cover (%):", lc.to_dict())
print(f"elevation: median {np.median(dem):.1f} m, 90 % of the district below {np.percentile(dem, 90):.1f} m")
print(f"surface water: {np.nanmean(occ > 0):.1%} of the district was ever water (1984-2020); {np.nanmean(occ >= 50):.1%} is water at least half the time")

# Side-by-side maps of land cover, elevation, and long-term water occurrence
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
cmap = plt.matplotlib.colors.ListedColormap(["#006400", "#ffbb22", "#ffff4c", "#f096ff", "#fa0000", "#b4b4b4", "#f0f0f0", "#0064c8", "#0096a0", "#00cf75", "#fae6a0"])
lc_img = np.where(inside, g0.values, np.nan)
codes = np.array(sorted(classes))
idx = np.searchsorted(codes, np.nan_to_num(lc_img, nan=10)).astype(float); idx[~inside] = np.nan
ax[0].imshow(idx, cmap=cmap, vmin=-0.5, vmax=10.5, interpolation="nearest"); ax[0].set_title("ESA WorldCover 2021")
im = ax[1].imshow(np.where(inside, grids["cop-dem-glo-30"].values, np.nan), cmap="terrain", vmin=0, vmax=40); ax[1].set_title("Copernicus DEM (m)")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.7)
im = ax[2].imshow(np.where(inside, occ_grid, np.nan), cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=100); ax[2].set_title("JRC water occurrence (%)")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax[2], shrink=0.7)
for a in ax:
    a.set_axis_off()
plt.suptitle("Sunamganj district from Planetary Computer global layers (30 m)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









Three global layers describe Sunamganj (3,693 km²) without processing a single image:

Land cover: cropland 57.6%, herbaceous wetland 21.4%, tree cover 12.7%, permanent water 6.5%.
Elevation: a median of only 5.1 m, with 90% of the district below 9.8 m.
Surface water: 78.7% of the district was water at some time between 1984 and 2020, and 36.4% is water at least half the time.

Most of the cropland is therefore seasonally flooded: haor fields carry one Boro rice crop in the dry season and lie under water in the monsoon, the cycle seen in the NDVI series of Notebook 08_06. The DEM took longest to load (19.5 s, four 1° tiles at full 30 m resolution); the single-tile layers took about 3 s each.

title: Cloud Platforms: Planetary Computer, Earth Engine and Copernicus openEO
text:
Server-side processing with openEO
openEO is an open standard API for Earth observation processing, implemented by several back ends, including the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem. A client builds a process graph (load a collection, filter, compute NDVI, reduce over time) and sends it to the back end, which runs it next to the data and returns only the result. Discovery works without an account.


Code
# Connect to Copernicus openEO and describe available collections and processes
t0 = time.perf_counter()
con = openeo.connect("https://openeo.dataspace.copernicus.eu")
collections = con.list_collection_ids()
processes = con.list_processes()
s2 = con.describe_collection("SENTINEL2_L2A")
print(f"connected in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s: {len(collections)} collections, {len(processes)} processes")
print("SENTINEL2_L2A temporal extent:", s2["extent"]["temporal"]["interval"][0], "| bands:", len(s2["cube:dimensions"]["bands"]["values"]))

# Build a process graph for clear-sky median NDVI (not executed yet)
cube_oe = con.load_collection("SENTINEL2_L2A", spatial_extent=dict(zip(["west", "south", "east", "north"], AOI)),
                              temporal_extent=["2024-01-01", "2024-03-31"], bands=["B04", "B08", "SCL"], max_cloud_cover=20)
scl = cube_oe.band("SCL")
clear_oe = (scl == 4) | (scl == 5)
ndvi_oe = cube_oe.ndvi(red="B04", nir="B08").mask(~clear_oe).reduce_dimension(dimension="t", reducer="median")
graph = json.loads(ndvi_oe.to_json())["process_graph"]
print(f"process graph: {len(graph)} nodes ->", [n["process_id"] for n in graph.values()])
_ = (OUT / "openeo_ndvi_median.json").write_text(ndvi_oe.to_json())


connected in 7.3 s: 138 collections, 146 processes
SENTINEL2_L2A temporal extent: ['2015-06-27T10:25:31Z', None] | bands: 21
process graph: 5 nodes -> ['load_collection', 'ndvi', 'reduce_dimension', 'mask', 'reduce_dimension']




Code
# Execution needs a (free) CDSE account. Set GEOLATTICE_OPENEO=1 after `con.authenticate_oidc()` has been done once
# interactively; the stored refresh token is then reused.
if os.environ.get("GEOLATTICE_OPENEO") == "1":
    con.authenticate_oidc()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    ndvi_oe.download(OUT / "openeo_ndvi_median.tif", format="GTiff")
    print(f"openEO result downloaded in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")
else:
    print("openEO execution skipped (no account configured). The process graph above is complete and can be run as is.")


openEO execution skipped (no account configured). The process graph above is complete and can be run as is.


Without an account, openEO on Copernicus Data Space exposed 138 collections and 146 processes, and accepted the composite of Section 5 as a five-node process graph:

load the collection;
compute NDVI;
reduce the scene classification band;
mask clouds;
take the median over time.

The graph, saved as JSON, is the complete, portable description of the analysis. Any openEO back end that offers the collection can run it. Execution, the only step that needs an account, was skipped here, as was the Earth Engine computation below.

title: Cloud Platforms: Planetary Computer, Earth Engine and Copernicus openEO
text:
Google Earth Engine
Earth Engine works the same way: Python objects describe a computation, which runs on Google’s servers when a result is requested. It needs a Google Cloud project registered for Earth Engine (free for research and non-commercial use) and a one-time ee.Authenticate(). The cell runs only when a project is configured in EE_PROJECT; the code is the Earth Engine version of Section 5. Note that Earth Engine’s COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED collection has already removed the offset of Section 4, another provider convention to check.


Code
# Optional Earth Engine run when EE_PROJECT is set in the environment
project = os.environ.get("EE_PROJECT")
try:
    if not project:
        raise RuntimeError("EE_PROJECT is not set")
    ee.Initialize(project=project)
    region = ee.Geometry.Rectangle(AOI)

    # Mask cloudy pixels and compute NDVI on Sentinel-2 SR
    def mask_and_ndvi(img):
        scl = img.select("SCL")
        clear = scl.eq(4).Or(scl.eq(5))
        return img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("ndvi").updateMask(clear)

    col = (ee.ImageCollection("COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED").filterBounds(region)
           .filterDate("2024-01-01", "2024-04-01").filter(ee.Filter.lt("CLOUDY_PIXEL_PERCENTAGE", 20)))
    median = col.map(mask_and_ndvi).median()
    stats = median.reduceRegion(ee.Reducer.median(), region, scale=10, maxPixels=1e9).getInfo()
    print(f"Earth Engine: {col.size().getInfo()} images; median NDVI {stats['ndvi']:.3f} "
          f"(odc-stac on Planetary Computer: {float(composite.median()):.3f})")
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"Earth Engine skipped: {exc}. To run it: create a Cloud project registered for Earth Engine, "
          "run ee.Authenticate() once, and set EE_PROJECT.")


Earth Engine skipped: EE_PROJECT is not set. To run it: create a Cloud project registered for Earth Engine, run ee.Authenticate() once, and set EE_PROJECT.

title: Cloud Platforms: Planetary Computer, Earth Engine and Copernicus openEO
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Catalogue platforms (STAC + COG) bring the data to your code; server-side platforms bring your code to the data.
The same product can carry different values on different platforms; read the processing baseline and the provider’s offset convention before mixing sources.
odc-stac loads only the bands, area and resolution you ask for, lazily, from any STAC API.
Global analysis-ready layers (WorldCover, Copernicus DEM, JRC water) answer many questions without processing imagery at all.
openEO and Earth Engine express the analysis as a graph run by the provider; discovery and graph building are free, execution needs an account.

What we found

The catalogues: Planetary Computer, Earth Search and Copernicus Data Space found the same 6 dates over Bogra, but returned different item counts (7, 6, 6), identifiers and file locations.
The offset: Planetary Computer’s Sentinel-2 DN are 1,000 higher than Earth Search’s for the same scene. Ignoring the offset cut median NDVI from 0.406 to 0.224; applying Earth Search’s metadata offset made 77% of NDVI values impossible.
The composite: odc-stac built a cloud-masked composite of 9 dates at 10 m in 18.5 s.
Sunamganj: 57.6% cropland, a median elevation of 5.1 m, and 78.7% of the district water at some time since 1984.
openEO and Earth Engine: the openEO graph was built (5 nodes) and the Earth Engine code was written; both need accounts to execute.

Exercises

Repeat Section 4 for a scene from 2021 (processing baseline 03.xx). What changes?
Build the composite of Section 5 from Earth Search instead of Planetary Computer with odc-stac. Which band names and offset handling must change? Compare the two composites pixel by pixel.
Compute the share of Sunamganj that is cropland and water at least 25 % of the time. What does it say about Boro rice in the haors?
Add Sentinel-1 RTC (sentinel-1-rtc on Planetary Computer) for August 2024 and map open water in Sunamganj by thresholding VV backscatter (Notebook 08_11 does this in full).
With a CDSE account, run the openEO graph of Section 7 and compare its median NDVI with Section 5.

References

Microsoft Planetary Computer. https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com
Earth Search by Element 84. https://element84.com/earth-search/
Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem. https://dataspace.copernicus.eu
Schramm, M. et al. (2021). The openEO API: Harmonising the use of Earth observation cloud services using virtual data cube functionalities. Remote Sensing, 13(6), 1125.
Gorelick, N. et al. (2017). Google Earth Engine: Planetary-scale geospatial analysis for everyone. Remote Sensing of Environment, 202, 18-27.
ESA (2022). Sentinel-2 processing baseline 04.00: provision of negative radiometric values (BOA_ADD_OFFSET).
Zanaga, D. et al. (2022). ESA WorldCover 10 m 2021 v200. Zenodo.
Pekel, J.-F. et al. (2016). High-resolution mapping of global surface water and its long-term changes. Nature, 540, 418-422.

title: Web Apps for Geospatial Data: Streamlit, Panel and Solara
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README. It also uses panel, psutil, solara, which no GeoLattice option installs: pip install panel psutil solara.


Code
# Imports and paths for Streamlit, Panel, and Solara dashboard apps
%matplotlib inline
import importlib
import inspect
import socket
import subprocess
import sys
import time
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import os
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

Three ways to build a Python web app

All three serve a page whose widgets talk to a Python process over a WebSocket: each browser tab is a session on the server, and the Python code runs on the server, not in the browser.

title: Web Apps for Geospatial Data: Streamlit, Panel and Solara
section: Design: a logic module and thin user interfaces
text:
Design: a logic module and thin user interfaces
The data loading, the map and the charts live in apps/bd_dashboard.py, a module with no web framework in it. Each app only arranges widgets and calls these functions. This makes the logic testable with plain Python, lets the three apps share it, and keeps a later change of framework cheap. The module also counts its function calls (CALLS), which Section 8 uses.


Code
# Inspect the shared bd_dashboard logic module (public functions and map variables)

    if not name.startswith("_") and f.__module__ == "bd_dashboard":
        print(f"  {name}{inspect.signature(f)}")
print("map variables:", list(bd.VARIABLES))

title: Web Apps for Geospatial Data: Streamlit, Panel and Solara
text:
Preparing data for an app
An app should open in a second. The raw inputs would take far longer: 572 NDVI images (368 MB in memory) and district boundaries with a million vertices. Everything the app shows can be computed in advance: the mean NDVI of each district on each date, the long-term mean and trend of each district’s annual NDVI peak, and boundaries simplified for display. The app then reads two small Parquet files.


Code
# Build district NDVI time series and trend stats; write compact Parquet for the apps
t0 = time.perf_counter()
# Load districts and the full MODIS NDVI stack into memory
districts = gpd.read_file(WEB / "08_03_outputs" / "districts.gpkg")
files = sorted(MODIS.glob("ndvi_*.tif"), key=lambda p: (int(p.stem.split("_")[1]), int(p.stem.split("_")[2])))
dates = pd.to_datetime([f"{p.stem.split('_')[1]}-{p.stem.split('_')[2]}" for p in files], format="%Y-%j")
with rasterio.open(files[0]) as src:
    crs, transform, shape = src.crs, src.transform, src.shape
cube = np.stack([rasterio.open(f).read(1) for f in files])                  # NDVI x 10,000; 0 = outside
raw_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
# Per-district mean NDVI series and Theil-Sen trend of annual peaks
years = np.arange(2001, 2025)
i, j = np.triu_indices(len(years), 1)
series, stats = [], []
for name, geom in zip(districts.district, districts.to_crs(crs).geometry):
    inside = geometry_mask([mapping(geom)], out_shape=shape, transform=transform, invert=True)
    v = cube[:, inside].astype("float32")
    v[v == 0] = np.nan
    mean = np.nanmean(v, axis=1) / 1e4
    series.append(pd.DataFrame({"district": name, "date": dates, "ndvi": mean.round(4)}))
    peak = pd.Series(mean, index=dates).groupby(lambda d: d.year).max().reindex(years).values
    stats.append({"district": name, "ndvi_max_mean": np.nanmean(peak),
                  "ndvi_trend": np.nanmedian((peak[j] - peak[i]) / (years[j] - years[i])) * 10})   # Theil-Sen, per decade
ndvi_long = pd.concat(series, ignore_index=True)
table = districts.merge(pd.DataFrame(stats), on="district")
table["density"] = table.population / table.area_km2
table["rice_t_km2"] = table.rice_t / table.area_km2
simple = gpd.GeoSeries(shapely.coverage_simplify(table.to_crs(32646).geometry.values, 500), crs=32646).to_crs(4326)
table = table.set_geometry(shapely.set_precision(simple.values, 1e-4)).set_crs(4326, allow_override=True)
table.to_parquet(OUT / "districts.parquet")
ndvi_long.to_parquet(OUT / "district_ndvi.parquet")
prep_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
# Time how long the prepared Parquet loads take in the app module
bd.load_districts(); bd.load_ndvi()
app_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0
pd.DataFrame({"what": ["raw inputs (572 GeoTIFFs + boundaries)", "prepared app data (2 Parquet files)"],
              "size": [f"{cube.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB in memory, {districts.geometry.count_coordinates().sum():,} vertices",
                       f"{sum(p.stat().st_size for p in OUT.glob('*.parquet')) / 1e3:.0f} kB on disk, "
                       f"{table.geometry.count_coordinates().sum():,} vertices"],
              "load seconds": [round(raw_seconds, 2), round(app_seconds, 3)]}).assign(
    note=["", f"preparation took {prep_seconds:.1f} s, once"])

Preparation took 2.1 s, once. The app then loads 288 kB (two Parquet files) in 0.03 s, against 3.1 s and 368 MB for the raw rasters, and draws 16,559 vertices instead of 1.06 million.
The new trend variable is worth a look:

Annual peak NDVI rose in 62 of the 64 districts between 2001 and 2024. The largest gains, about +0.067 per decade, are in the north-west (Naogaon, Natore, Pabna) and in Faridpur.
Only Bagerhat (−0.013) and Satkhira (−0.005) declined, both in the south-western coastal belt.
The forested hill districts (Khagrachhari, Rangamati) were already at the top (mean peak about 0.82-0.84) and barely changed.
The trend is unrelated to population density (Spearman 0.03).

One data gap shows up as well: Bagerhat’s rice production is 0 in the district table, which points to a missing row in the rice data joined in Notebook 08_03 rather than a real value.

title: Web Apps for Geospatial Data: Streamlit, Panel and Solara
text:
The Streamlit app
A Streamlit app is a script. Widgets return their current values; the script then draws the page. When the user changes a widget, Streamlit reruns the whole script with the new value. @st.cache_data keeps the data loaders from running again.


Code
# Show the Streamlit app source
display(Code(filename=str(APPS / "bd_streamlit.py"), language="python"))


"""
Bangladesh district explorer, Streamlit version (Notebook 08_07).

Run:  streamlit run bd_streamlit.py
"""

import streamlit as st
from streamlit_folium import st_folium

import bd_dashboard as bd

st.set_page_config(page_title="Bangladesh district explorer", page_icon="🌾", layout="wide")


@st.cache_data                     # read once per server process, shared by every session
def districts():
    return bd.load_districts()


@st.cache_data
def ndvi():
    return bd.load_ndvi()


gdf, nd = districts(), ndvi()

with st.sidebar:
    st.header("Select")
    division = st.selectbox("Division", ["All"] + sorted(gdf.division.unique()), key="division")
    names = bd.district_list(gdf, division)
    district = st.selectbox("District", names, index=names.index("Bogra") if "Bogra" in names else 0, key="district")
    variable = st.radio("Map variable", list(bd.VARIABLES), format_func=bd.VARIABLES.get, key="variable")
    st.caption("Data: BBS poverty and census tables, DAE rice statistics, MODIS NDVI 2000-2024 (Notebooks 08_03, 08_06).")

st.title("Bangladesh district explorer")
card = bd.district_card(gdf, district)
c1, c2, c3, c4 = st.columns(4)
c1.metric("Poverty", f"{card['poverty_pct']:.1f} %" if card["poverty_pct"] is not None else "n/a",
          f"rank {card['poverty_rank']} of 64" if card["poverty_rank"] else None, delta_color="off")
c2.metric("Population density", f"{card['density']:,.0f} per km²" if card["density"] else "n/a")
c3.metric("Rice 2018-19", f"{card['rice_kt']:,.0f} kt", f"rank {card['rice_rank']} of 64 per km²", delta_color="off")
c4.metric("NDVI trend", f"{card['ndvi_trend']:+.3f} / decade", f"rank {card['ndvi_trend_rank']} of 64", delta_color="off")

left, right = st.columns([1, 1])
with left:
    st_folium(bd.choropleth(gdf, variable, district), height=480, use_container_width=True, returned_objects=[])
with right:
    st.plotly_chart(bd.ndvi_figure(nd, district), width="stretch")
    st.plotly_chart(bd.seasonal_figure(nd, district), width="stretch")



Streamlit’s AppTest runs the script headless, as a user session would, and lets a test change widgets and read what the page shows. We count which functions of the logic module each interaction runs.


Code
# Drive Streamlit via AppTest: open app, pick district/map variable/division; record call counts
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

def take():
    "Return and reset the call counts of the logic module."
    c = dict(bd.CALLS); bd.CALLS.clear(); return c

counts = {}
bd.CALLS.clear()
at = AppTest.from_file(str(APPS / "bd_streamlit.py"), default_timeout=60)
steps = [("open the app", lambda: at.run()),
         ("choose district Dhaka", lambda: at.selectbox(key="district").select("Dhaka").run()),
         ("switch map to NDVI trend", lambda: at.radio(key="variable").set_value("ndvi_trend").run()),
         ("choose division Sylhet", lambda: at.selectbox(key="division").select("Sylhet").run())]
for label, action in steps:
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); action()
    counts[("Streamlit", label)] = {"ms": (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, **take()}
print("errors:", list(at.exception))
print("metrics after the last step:", {m.label: m.value for m in at.metric})
print("district selected after choosing Sylhet:", at.selectbox(key="district").value)
pd.DataFrame(counts).T.fillna(0).round(0)

title: Web Apps for Geospatial Data: Streamlit, Panel and Solara
text:
The Panel app
Panel separates the parts: widgets, output panes and the functions that fill them. Each function declares which widgets it depends on (@pn.depends(..., watch=True)), and Panel calls it only when one of them changes. build() returns the template and the widgets, so a test can drive them.


Code
# Show the Panel app source
display(Code(filename=str(APPS / "bd_panel.py"), language="python"))


"""
Bangladesh district explorer, Panel version (Notebook 08_07).

Run:  panel serve bd_panel.py
"""

import panel as pn

import bd_dashboard as bd

pn.extension("plotly", sizing_mode="stretch_width")


@pn.cache                          # read once per server process, shared by every session
def data():
    return bd.load_districts(), bd.load_ndvi()


def build():
    """Create the widgets, panes and template; return (template, widgets) so tests can drive them."""
    gdf, nd = data()
    division = pn.widgets.Select(name="Division", options=["All"] + sorted(gdf.division.unique()), value="All")
    district = pn.widgets.Select(name="District", options=bd.district_list(gdf), value="Bogra")
    variable = pn.widgets.RadioButtonGroup(name="Map variable", options={v: k for k, v in bd.VARIABLES.items()},
                                           value="poverty_pct", orientation="vertical", button_type="light")

    cards = pn.pane.Markdown()
    map_pane = pn.pane.plot.Folium(height=480)
    ts_pane = pn.pane.Plotly(height=330)
    season_pane = pn.pane.Plotly(height=280)

    # Each output is recomputed only when one of its own inputs changes.
    @pn.depends(division, watch=True)
    def _filter(div):
        names = bd.district_list(gdf, div)
        district.options = names
        if district.value not in names:
            district.value = names[0]

    @pn.depends(district, watch=True)
    def _district(name):
        c = bd.district_card(gdf, name)
        pov = f"{c['poverty_pct']:.1f} % (rank {c['poverty_rank']} of 64)" if c["poverty_pct"] is not None else "n/a"
        cards.object = (f"### {name}, {c['division']} division\n"
                        f"**Poverty** {pov} · **Density** {c['density']:,.0f} per km² · "
                        f"**Rice** {c['rice_kt']:,.0f} kt · **NDVI trend** {c['ndvi_trend']:+.3f} per decade")
        ts_pane.object = bd.ndvi_figure(nd, name)
        season_pane.object = bd.seasonal_figure(nd, name)

    @pn.depends(variable, district, watch=True)
    def _map(var, name):
        map_pane.object = bd.choropleth(gdf, var, name)

    _district(district.value)              # first render
    _map(variable.value, district.value)
    template = pn.template.FastListTemplate(
        title="Bangladesh district explorer",
        sidebar=[division, district, pn.pane.Markdown("**Map variable**"), variable,
                 pn.pane.Markdown("Data: BBS, DAE, MODIS NDVI 2000-2024 (Notebooks 08_03, 08_06).")],
        main=[cards, pn.Row(map_pane, pn.Column(ts_pane, season_pane))],
        accent="#2c7fb8")
    return template, {"division": division, "district": district, "variable": variable,
                      "cards": cards, "map": map_pane, "timeseries": ts_pane, "seasonal": season_pane}


if __name__.startswith("bokeh"):    # `panel serve` runs this file once per browser session
    build()[0].servable()

title: Web Apps for Geospatial Data: Streamlit, Panel and Solara
text:
The Solara app
Solara builds the page from components, functions decorated with @solara.component. State is held in solara.reactive variables; when one changes, the components that read it run again. Inside a component, use_memo keeps an expensive result until one of its listed dependencies changes, much as pn.depends does in Panel.


Code
# Show the Solara app source
display(Code(filename=str(APPS / "bd_solara.py"), language="python"))


"""
Bangladesh district explorer, Solara version (Notebook 08_07).

Run:  solara run bd_solara.py
"""

import solara

import bd_dashboard as bd

GDF, NDVI = bd.load_districts(), bd.load_ndvi()     # module level: loaded once per server process

# Reactive state; Solara keeps a separate copy for every browser session.
division = solara.reactive("All")
district = solara.reactive("Bogra")
variable = solara.reactive("poverty_pct")


@solara.component
def Cards(name: str):
    c = solara.use_memo(lambda: bd.district_card(GDF, name), dependencies=[name])
    pov = f"{c['poverty_pct']:.1f} % (rank {c['poverty_rank']} of 64)" if c["poverty_pct"] is not None else "n/a"
    solara.Markdown(f"### {name}, {c['division']} division\n"
                    f"**Poverty** {pov} · **Density** {c['density']:,.0f} per km² · "
                    f"**Rice** {c['rice_kt']:,.0f} kt · **NDVI trend** {c['ndvi_trend']:+.3f} per decade")


@solara.component
def Page():
    names = solara.use_memo(lambda: bd.district_list(GDF, division.value), dependencies=[division.value])
    if district.value not in names:
        district.set(names[0])
    # use_memo: recompute only when the listed inputs change
    m = solara.use_memo(lambda: bd.choropleth(GDF, variable.value, district.value)._repr_html_(),
                        dependencies=[variable.value, district.value])
    ts = solara.use_memo(lambda: bd.ndvi_figure(NDVI, district.value), dependencies=[district.value])
    season = solara.use_memo(lambda: bd.seasonal_figure(NDVI, district.value), dependencies=[district.value])

    solara.Title("Bangladesh district explorer")
    labels = {label: key for key, label in bd.VARIABLES.items()}
    with solara.Columns([1, 2, 2]):
        with solara.Column():                       # controls (a plain column works at any screen width)
            solara.Markdown("## Bangladesh district explorer")
            solara.Select("Division", values=["All"] + sorted(GDF.division.unique()), value=division)
            solara.Select("District", values=names, value=district)
            solara.Select("Map variable", values=list(labels), value=bd.VARIABLES[variable.value],
                          on_value=lambda label: variable.set(labels[label]))
            solara.Markdown("Data: BBS, DAE, MODIS NDVI 2000-2024 (Notebooks 08_03, 08_06).")
        with solara.Column():
            Cards(district.value)
            solara.HTML(tag="div", unsafe_innerHTML=m)
        with solara.Column():
            solara.FigurePlotly(ts)
            solara.FigurePlotly(season)

We start all three, wait until they answer, and record start-up time and memory. Each server is a separate process.


Code
# Launch Streamlit, Panel, and Solara servers; record start-up time, memory, and first HTML size
# Helpers: free TCP port and process RSS including children
def free_port():
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); return s.getsockname()[1]

def rss_mb(proc):
    p = psutil.Process(proc.pid)
    return sum(q.memory_info().rss for q in [p] + p.children(recursive=True)) / 1e6

# Start each framework server and wait until healthy
ports = {name: free_port() for name in ["Streamlit", "Panel", "Solara"]}
commands = {
    "Streamlit": ([sys.executable, "-m", "streamlit", "run", "bd_streamlit.py", "--server.port", str(ports["Streamlit"]),
                   "--server.headless", "true", "--browser.gatherUsageStats", "false"], "/_stcore/health", "/"),
    "Panel": ([sys.executable, "-m", "panel", "serve", "bd_panel.py", "--port", str(ports["Panel"]), "--address", "127.0.0.1",
               "--allow-websocket-origin", f"127.0.0.1:{ports['Panel']}", "--allow-websocket-origin", f"localhost:{ports['Panel']}"],
              "/bd_panel", "/bd_panel"),
    "Solara": ([sys.executable, "-m", "solara", "run", "bd_solara.py", "--port", str(ports["Solara"]), "--host", "127.0.0.1",
                "--no-open", "--production"], "/", "/"),
}
servers, rows = {}, []
for name, (cmd, health, page) in commands.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, cwd=APPS, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    base = f"http://127.0.0.1:{ports[name]}"
    while time.perf_counter() - t0 < 120:
        try:
            if httpx.get(base + health, timeout=5).status_code == 200:
                break
        except httpx.HTTPError:
            pass
        time.sleep(0.2)
    started = time.perf_counter() - t0
    idle = rss_mb(proc)
    r = httpx.get(base + page, timeout=60)
    servers[name] = (proc, base + page)
    rows.append({"framework": name, "start-up s": round(started, 1), "memory at start MB": round(idle),
                 "page status": r.status_code, "first HTML kB": round(len(r.content) / 1e3, 1)})
startup = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("framework")

title: Web Apps for Geospatial Data: Streamlit, Panel and Solara
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Streamlit reruns the whole script on every interaction; Panel and Solara rerun only what depends on the changed input. Caching (st.cache_data, pn.cache, use_memo) is how each avoids repeated work.
Put data and figures in a plain module; the app is a thin layer that is easy to test and to port.
Precompute what the app shows; an app should load kilobytes.
Test apps headlessly: AppTest for Streamlit, widget values for Panel, solara.render for Solara.
Each browser tab is a server-side session; memory and CPU per session decide how many users a server can hold.

What we built and measured

One logic module (133 lines) and three thin apps: Streamlit (49 lines), Panel and Solara.
App data prepared once, 288 kB, loading in 0.03 s instead of 3.1 s.
NDVI peaks rose in 62 of 64 districts from 2001 to 2024; only two coastal districts in the south-west declined.
Switching the map variable rebuilt 4 outputs in Streamlit and 1 in Panel and Solara.
Start-up: Streamlit 0.8 s and 82 MB, Solara 1.3 s and 212 MB, Panel 2.7 s and 276 MB (before any session).

Exercises

Add @st.cache_data to wrappers around bd.choropleth, bd.ndvi_figure and bd.seasonal_figure in the Streamlit app, and repeat the counts of Section 5. What changes, and what does the cache cost in memory?
Add a “compare with” district selector to all three apps that overlays a second district on the NDVI chart. How many lines did each framework need?
Make the Panel app show the districts with pn.pane.DataFrame sorted by the map variable, linked to the district selector.
Replace the Folium map in the Solara app with ipyleaflet (or leafmap) and make a click on a district select it.
Convert the Panel app to WebAssembly with panel convert apps/bd_panel.py --to pyodide-worker and list which dependencies prevent it from running in the browser.

        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{needed} is missing: run Notebooks 08_01 and 08_03 first")

http = httpx.Client(timeout=300)

def get(url, show=True, **params):
    "GET a URL; print status, type and size; return the response."
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = http.get(url, params=params or None)
    if show:
        print(f"{r.status_code} {r.headers.get('content-type', '-'):38s} {len(r.content):>11,} bytes "
              f"{(time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000:7.0f} ms  {r.url.path}{'?' + r.url.query.decode() if r.url.query else ''}")
    return r

def web_ready(gdf, tolerance=250, digits=5):
    "Coverage-simplify in UTM 46N and round coordinates (Notebook 08_04)."
    g = gdf.to_crs(32646)
    s = gpd.GeoSeries(shapely.coverage_simplify(g.geometry.values, tolerance), crs=32646).to_crs(4326)
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(gdf.drop(columns="geometry"),
                            geometry=shapely.set_precision(s.values, 10.0 ** -digits), crs=4326)

title: Serving Maps: Tiles and OGC APIs
text:
Map-service standards









Standard
Request
Returns
Typical use




WMS (OGC Web Map Service, 1999)
A bounding box, size and layers
One rendered image per request
Classic GIS servers; any extent, no caching


WMTS (OGC, 2010) / TMS
A tile in a fixed grid
Pre-cut image tiles
Cached basemaps in desktop GIS


XYZ tiles (/{z}/{x}/{y}.png)
Zoom, column, row in Web Mercator
256 × 256 image tiles
Every web map; de facto standard


TileJSON
tilejson.json
Tile URL template, bounds, zoom range
Lets a client configure itself


Vector tiles (MVT)
A tile in the XYZ grid
Clipped, simplified vector features (Protobuf)
Styled in the browser; MapLibre, Mapbox


PMTiles
HTTP range requests on one file
Vector or raster tiles plus an index
Tile sets without a tile server


OGC API: Features (2019)
/collections/{id}/items?bbox=...
GeoJSON features, paged
Data access for programs, QGIS, ArcGIS


OGC API: Tiles / Maps (2022-23)
/collections/{id}/tiles/..., /map
Tiles / map images with metadata
Modern successors of WMTS and WMS



The OGC API family replaces the XML-based W*S services with resource URLs, JSON and an OpenAPI description, the same style as any modern web API.
Tiles can be static (rendered once, stored as files, served by any web server or a CDN) or dynamic (rendered from the source data when requested). geolattice.web does both: make_xyz_tiles writes static pyramids, and create_app builds a server for dynamic tiles and OGC API: Features (Starlette, run with uvicorn).

title: Serving Maps: Tiles and OGC APIs
text:
Dynamic tiles: rendering on request
A dynamic tile server keeps only the source raster and renders each tile when it is asked for: it reads the pixels under the tile, warps them to Web Mercator, applies a colour map and encodes a PNG. create_app builds such a server. start_server runs it in the background, so the notebook can keep working while it serves (on a real server you would use web.serve(app) or uvicorn).


Code
# Start a dynamic tile server and compare latency to static PNG tiles
tile_app = web.create_app(rasters={"ndvi": {"path": ndvi_path, "colormap": "RdYlGn", "rescale": (-0.1, 0.9)}},
                          title="Syracuse NDVI")
tile_server = web.start_server(tile_app)
print(tile_server)
for path in ["/tiles", "/tiles/ndvi/tilejson.json"]:
    get(tile_server.url + path)

dynamic_ms = []
for t in tiles14:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = http.get(f"{tile_server.url}/tiles/ndvi/{t.z}/{t.x}/{t.y}.png")
    dynamic_ms.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
print(f"dynamic tiles: {len(dynamic_ms)} requests, median {np.median(dynamic_ms):.1f} ms, max {max(dynamic_ms):.1f} ms;"
      f" Cache-Control: {r.headers['cache-control']}")
empty = get(f"{tile_server.url}/tiles/ndvi/14/0/0.png")


BackgroundServer(http://127.0.0.1:34797)
200 application/json                               228 bytes       2 ms  /tiles
200 application/json                               241 bytes       1 ms  /tiles/ndvi/tilejson.json
dynamic tiles: 30 requests, median 33.6 ms, max 84.0 ms; Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
204 -                                                0 bytes       2 ms  /tiles/ndvi/14/0/0.png


Static tiles came back in a median 3.0 ms: the server only reads a file. The dynamic server needed a median 34 ms per tile to read, warp, colour and encode it, about ten times longer, but it stores nothing beyond the 8.6 MB source raster. A tile outside the raster returns 204 No Content, which map libraries treat as an empty tile, and every tile carries Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 so browsers and CDNs can reuse it.

Why the source must be a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF
A tile server rarely has the raster on its own disk; it reads it from object storage. Then the file layout decides how many bytes each tile costs. We serve two versions of the same Sentinel-2 band stack over HTTP, the plain tiled GeoTIFF downloaded in 08_01 (12 MB, no overviews) and the COG made from it (16 MB, with overviews), and count what one tile at each zoom transfers.
The file server runs in a separate process (subprocess=True). rasterio, which render_tile uses, ships its own GDAL and holds Python’s global interpreter lock while it waits for the network, so it would deadlock against a file server running in this same process.


Code
# Compare plain GeoTIFF vs COG byte reads when tiles are rendered on the fly
files_srv = web.static_server(WEB, subprocess=True)
layers = {"plain": "s2_syracuse_2025/S2C_18TVN_20250723_0_L2A/stack.tif",
          "cog": "08_01_outputs/stack_deflate_2.tif"}
for name, rel in layers.items():
    size = (WEB / rel).stat().st_size
    import rasterio
    with rasterio.open(WEB / rel) as src:
        print(f"{name:5s}: {size / 1e6:5.1f} MB, blocks {src.block_shapes[0]}, overviews {src.overviews(1) or 'none'}")

cog_app = web.create_app(rasters={n: {"path": f"{files_srv.url}/{rel}", "bands": [3, 2, 1], "rescale": (0, 2500)}
                                  for n, rel in layers.items()})
import os
os.environ["CPL_VSIL_CURL_NON_CACHED"] = f"/vsicurl/{files_srv.url}"     # measure each tile from scratch
rows = []
with web.start_server(cog_app) as srv:
    for name in layers:
        for z in range(10, 15):
            t = web.lonlat_to_tile(-76.14, 43.04, z)
            files_srv.reset()
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            r = http.get(f"{srv.url}/tiles/{name}/{z}/{t.x}/{t.y}.png")
            ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
            s = files_srv.stats
            rows.append({"file": name, "zoom": z, "HTTP requests": s["requests"], "MB read": round(s["bytes"] / 1e6, 2),
                         "ms": round(ms)})
del os.environ["CPL_VSIL_CURL_NON_CACHED"]
cog_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="zoom", columns="file", values=["MB read", "HTTP requests"])

At zoom 10, where one tile covers the whole image, the plain GeoTIFF had to read 10.0 MB of its 12.2 MB (every full-resolution pixel under the tile) in 7 requests, while the COG read 0.82 MB from its 4× overview. The COG kept using overviews down to zoom 12. At zooms 13-14, where tiles are close to full resolution, the COG read more (3.24 and 1.66 MB against 1.66 and 0.52 MB): its blocks are 512 × 512 pixels instead of 256 × 256, so each block it fetches covers more ground than one small tile needs. Smaller internal blocks favour high-zoom tiles; overviews are what make zoomed-out views affordable. Note also that the plain file needed up to 23 HTTP requests per tile, the COG at most 6.
While building this comparison we found and fixed two problems in geolattice.web: render_tile warped from full resolution even when the COG had overviews (a zoomed-out tile of a large remote COG took many seconds), and a single rescale pair given as a list was rejected for RGB rasters only when the first tile was requested. Tiles now read from the coarsest suitable overview, and create_app checks the band and rescale settings when it starts.


Straight from the cloud
The same server can render tiles from a COG anywhere on the internet. Here it serves the true-colour image of Sentinel-2 tile 18TVN (110 × 110 km) directly from Earth Search’s AWS bucket, with no download. Each request is timed twice: cold, and again once GDAL has cached the blocks.


Code
# Render tiles from a remote Sentinel-2 COG; time cold vs warm requests
TCI = ("https://sentinel-cogs.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/sentinel-s2-l2a-cogs/18/T/VN/2025/7/"
       "S2C_18TVN_20250723_0_L2A/TCI.tif")
try:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    remote_app = web.create_app(rasters={"s2": {"path": TCI, "rescale": (0, 255)}})
    print(f"app ready in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s (reads the COG header)")
    rows = []
    with web.start_server(remote_app) as srv:
        for z in [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]:
            t = web.lonlat_to_tile(-76.14, 43.04, z)
            for run in ["cold", "warm", "warm", "warm"]:
                t0 = time.perf_counter()
                r = http.get(f"{srv.url}/tiles/s2/{z}/{t.x}/{t.y}.png")
                rows.append({"zoom": z, "run": run, "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0, "status": r.status_code})
    remote = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot_table(index="zoom", columns="run", values="seconds", aggfunc="median")[["cold", "warm"]].round(2)
    remote.columns = ["cold (s)", "warm, median of 3 (s)"]
    display(remote)
except Exception as exc:                              # no network: the rest of the notebook still runs
    remote = None
    print("Remote COG not reachable:", type(exc).__name__, exc)

Every tile here crosses the internet to AWS us-west-2, so the times depend on the network and vary from run to run. In this run, cold tiles took between 0.05 and 3.4 s. Repeating a tile at zooms 12-14 brought it down to tens of milliseconds because GDAL caches the blocks it has read, while the zoomed-out tiles (zooms 9-11) stayed between about 0.8 and 1.3 s. A server in the same cloud region as the data, with a CDN in front of it, is how services such as Earth Search’s own viewers keep this fast.
Static or dynamic?









Static pyramid
Dynamic server




Latency per tile
Lowest (a file read)
Render time plus source reads


Storage
Grows 4× per zoom level
Only the source COG


New data / new colours
Re-render everything
Immediate; colour map and bands are request options in TiTiler-style servers


Hosting
Any static host or CDN; no server process
A running service (container, serverless function)


Best for
Fixed products viewed by many
Many scenes, analysis, changing styles



In practice the two are combined: a dynamic server behind a CDN that caches every tile the first time it is rendered. create_app sends Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 for that reason.

title: Serving Maps: Tiles and OGC APIs
text:
An OGC API: Features service
OGC API: Features turns each vector layer into a collection with a fixed set of URLs. We publish four collections: districts with poverty and population, all 5,160 unions, the arsenic fields and the California PM2.5 measurements, which have a date and so can be queried by time. Boundaries are coverage-simplified first (Notebook 08_04), because every response is GeoJSON.


Code
# Prepare vector layers and start an OGC API Features server
districts = web_ready(gpd.read_file(WEB / "08_03_outputs" / "districts.gpkg"))
unions = web_ready(gpd.read_file(BD / "Shapefiles" / "bd_union_GCS.shp")[["ADM4_EN", "ADM3_EN", "ADM2_EN", "ADM1_EN", "geometry"]], 100)
ars = pd.read_csv(BD / "bd_arsenic_data.csv")
fields = gpd.GeoDataFrame(ars[["ID", "WAs", "SAs", "GAs", "Variety", "Land_type"]],
                          geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(ars.Longitude, ars.Latitude), crs=4326)
pm = pd.read_csv(DATA / "00_shared" / "data_spatial_stat" / "CA_pm25_2025.csv")
pm25 = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"site": pm["Site ID"].astype(str), "county": pm.County,
                         "date": pd.to_datetime(pm.Date, format="%m/%d/%Y"),
                         "pm25": pm["Daily_PM2.5_ug_m3"], "aqi": pm.Daily_AQI},
                        geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(pm.Long, pm.Lat), crs=4326)
for name, g in [("districts", districts), ("unions", unions), ("fields", fields), ("pm25", pm25)]:
    print(f"{name:9s} {len(g):>6,} features, columns: {', '.join(c for c in g.columns if c != 'geometry')}")

feature_app = web.create_app(vectors={"districts": districts, "unions": unions, "fields": fields, "pm25": pm25},
                             title="Bangladesh and California sample data", default_limit=10, max_limit=10_000)
api = web.start_server(feature_app)
BASE = api.url
print(api)

The resource tree
A client starts at the landing page and follows links. The service lists the standards it implements at /conformance and describes itself in OpenAPI at /api, which tools turn into documentation or client code.

Items: paging, bounding boxes, attributes and time
/collections/{id}/items returns a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with numberMatched (all features that match), numberReturned (this page) and a next link while more remain. Clients page with limit and offset, or simply follow next.


Code
# Page through district items, then follow next links for Barisal unions
page = get(BASE + "/collections/districts/items", limit=3).json()
print("matched", page["numberMatched"], "| returned", page["numberReturned"], "| first:",
      [f["properties"]["district"] for f in page["features"]])
print("links:", [(l["rel"], l["href"].replace(BASE, "")) for l in page["links"]])

# follow `next` links through all unions in Barisal division, 200 at a time
url, n_pages, got = BASE + "/collections/unions/items?ADM1_EN=Barisal&limit=200", 0, []
while url:
    body = http.get(url).json()
    got += body["features"]; n_pages += 1
    url = next((l["href"] for l in body["links"] if l["rel"] == "next"), None)
print(f"Barisal: {len(got)} unions in {n_pages} pages (numberMatched {body['numberMatched']})")

      {"datetime": "2025-01-07T00:00:00Z/2025-01-13T23:59:59Z", "bbox": "-118.7,33.6,-117.6,34.4", "limit": 1000}),
     ("datetime: open end (from 25 Dec 2025)", "pm25", {"datetime": "2025-12-25T00:00:00Z/..", "limit": 1})]

for label, cid, params in q:

    body = r.json()
    rows.append({"query": label, "collection": cid, "numberMatched": body["numberMatched"],

la = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(http.get(f"{BASE}/collections/pm25/items", params=q[4][2]).json(), crs=4326)

Each filter is answered by the server, so only matching features travel:

the central-Dhaka box returned 123 unions (67 kB);
an attribute filter returned the 81 unions of Satkhira district, and 84 of the 263 fields grow the BR28 rice variety;
datetime selects by the collection’s date column: 154 sites reported on 1 July 2025, and an interval plus a box returned 130 measurements from Los Angeles-area sites for 7-13 January 2025. An open interval (2025-12-25T00:00:00Z/..) matched 1,111 rows; with limit=1 only one was sent.

The figure shows why time filters matter: that January week was the week of the Los Angeles wildfires. Daily PM2.5 reached 99.6 µg/m³ on 8 January, and the median across sites was 38.4 µg/m³ on 9 January, above the US 24-hour standard, before falling to 5.8-7.1 µg/m³ on 12-13 January. The datetime filter and the temporal extent in /collections were added to create_app while writing this notebook: OGC API: Features Core requires servers to accept datetime, and the earlier version rejected it as an unknown property.


Errors are part of the contract
A good API fails clearly, with the right status code and a message:


Code
# Probe common error cases (missing collection, bad params, unknown feature)
for path in ["/collections/rivers", "/collections/unions/items?bbox=90,23,91",
             "/collections/pm25/items?datetime=last-week", "/collections/unions/items?limit=0",
             "/collections/unions/items?colour=red", "/collections/unions/items/999999"]:
    r = http.get(BASE + path)
    print(r.status_code, f"{path:45s}", r.json().get("description", ""))

400 /collections/pm25/items?datetime=last-week    datetime must be an RFC 3339 instant or interval, e.g. 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z or 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z/..
400 /collections/unions/items?limit=0             limit must be a positive integer and offset a non-negative integer
400 /collections/unions/items?colour=red          Unknown property 'colour'
404 /collections/unions/items/999999              No feature '999999' in 'unions'

Every page is GeoJSON, so its size follows the geometry. For the unions:

    rows.append({"limit": limit, "MB": round(len(r.content) / 1e6, 2), "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2),
