Paging, bbox filters and simplified display geometry keep responses small; serve full-resolution geometry only to clients that need it for analysis.

title: Serving Maps: Tiles and OGC APIs
section: Using the service from GDAL, GeoPandas and OWSLib
text:
Using the service from GDAL, GeoPandas and OWSLib
The point of a standard is that clients written by others work without knowing anything about our server. Three independent ones:

GDAL’s OAPIF driver (and so QGIS, ArcGIS Pro via GDAL, ogr2ogr): opened with OAPIF: plus the URL;
GeoPandas, which reads a GeoJSON URL directly;
OWSLib, a Python client library for OGC services.



Code
# Query the feature API with GDAL/OGR and copy districts to a GeoPackage
ds = gdal.OpenEx("OAPIF:" + BASE, gdal.OF_VECTOR)
print("GDAL sees", [ds.GetLayer(i).GetName() for i in range(ds.GetLayerCount())])
lyr = ds.GetLayerByName("unions")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"unions: {lyr.GetFeatureCount():,} features, extent {[round(v, 2) for v in lyr.GetExtent()]}")
lyr.SetSpatialFilterRect(90.35, 23.70, 90.45, 23.82)
names = [f.GetField("ADM4_EN") for f in lyr]
print(f"GDAL bbox query: {len(names)} unions in central Dhaka, e.g. {sorted(set(names))[:4]} ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
lyr.SetSpatialFilter(None)
lyr.SetAttributeFilter("ADM2_EN = 'Satkhira'")
print("GDAL attribute filter, Satkhira unions:", lyr.GetFeatureCount())

# ogr2ogr: copy a collection from the service into a GeoPackage, as a desktop user would
t0 = time.perf_counter()
gdal.VectorTranslate(str(OUT / "from_api.gpkg"), "OAPIF:" + BASE, layers=["districts"], format="GPKG")
copied = gpd.read_file(OUT / "from_api.gpkg")
print(f"ogr2ogr copied {len(copied)} districts to from_api.gpkg in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
ds = None


GDAL sees ['districts', 'unions', 'fields', 'pm25']
unions: 5,160 features, extent [88.01, 92.68, 20.59, 26.63]
GDAL bbox query: 123 unions in central Dhaka, e.g. ['Aganagar', 'Badda', 'Beraid', 'Bhatara'] (0.0 s)
GDAL attribute filter, Satkhira unions: 81
ogr2ogr copied 64 districts to from_api.gpkg in 0.1 s




Code
# Read features with GeoPandas and OWSLib against the same OGC API endpoint
t0 = time.perf_counter()
gdf = gpd.read_file(f"{BASE}/collections/districts/items?limit=1000")
print(f"GeoPandas: {len(gdf)} districts, CRS {gdf.crs.to_string()}, in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
same = gdf.set_index("district").poverty_pct.sort_index().equals(districts.set_index("district").poverty_pct.sort_index())
print("poverty values identical to the source:", same)

oapi = Features(BASE)
print("OWSLib collections:", [c["id"] for c in oapi.collections()["collections"]])
fc = oapi.collection_items("fields", limit=500)
fields_back = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(fc, crs=4326)
print(f"OWSLib: {fc['numberReturned']} fields, mean water arsenic {fields_back.WAs.mean():.3f} mg/L "
      f"(source {fields.WAs.mean():.3f})")


GeoPandas: 64 districts, CRS EPSG:4326, in 0.05 s
poverty values identical to the source: True
OWSLib collections: ['districts', 'unions', 'fields', 'pm25']
OWSLib: 263 fields, mean water arsenic 0.130 mg/L (source 0.130)


All three clients worked against the service without any configuration beyond its URL:

GDAL found the four collections. Its bounding-box query returned the same 123 unions as our own request, its attribute filter the same 81 Satkhira unions, and ogr2ogr copied the 64 districts into a GeoPackage.
GeoPandas read the 64 districts, with poverty values identical to the source.
OWSLib listed the collections and read all 263 fields; their mean water arsenic, 0.130 mg/L, matches the source table.

Before this notebook create_app had no /api (OpenAPI) document, which OGC API. Features Core requires and the landing page must link as service-desc; it was added along with datetime.
In QGIS: Layer → Add Layer → Add WFS / OGC API: Features Layer, new connection, URL = the landing page. The collections appear as layers; QGIS sends bbox requests as you pan.

A map viewer
create_app also serves /viewer, a Leaflet page that draws every collection and tile layer. It reads each collection through the same /items URL as any other client.


Code
# Start a combined raster+vector app and open its built-in map viewer
viewer_app = web.create_app(
    rasters={"ndvi": {"path": ndvi_path, "colormap": "RdYlGn", "rescale": (-0.1, 0.9)}},
    vectors={"counties": gpd.read_file(DATA / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA" / "NY_County_GCS.shp")[["COUNTY", "geometry"]]
             .pipe(lambda g: g[g.COUNTY.isin([f"{c} County" for c in ["Onondaga", "Madison", "Cayuga", "Oswego", "Cortland"]])])},
    title="Syracuse NDVI and counties")
viewer = web.start_server(viewer_app)
display(IFrame(viewer.url + "/viewer", width="100%", height=450))



        
        


The viewer, like the other live maps in this notebook, is served by this notebook’s kernel and goes blank when the kernel stops.

title: Serving Maps: Tiles and OGC APIs
text:
One server, many requests
A map view fires dozens of tile requests at once, often while another client downloads features. create_app handles requests concurrently: features are encoded in worker threads, with geometry written by GEOS (shapely.to_geojson) rather than through Python dictionaries. But threads in one Python process share one interpreter lock (the GIL), so a CPU-heavy request still competes with everything else in that process. Production servers therefore run several worker processes.
We measure tile latency alone, and while another client (curl, in its own process) downloads all 5,160 unions at full resolution, the heaviest request this data allows. First with the server inside this notebook (one process, shared with the notebook itself), then with the same app run by uvicorn --workers 4 in separate processes.


Code
# Compare tile latency alone vs during a heavy download: in-process vs uvicorn workers
import socket
import subprocess
import sys

unions_full = gpd.read_file(BD / "Shapefiles" / "bd_union_GCS.shp")[["ADM4_EN", "ADM3_EN", "ADM2_EN", "geometry"]]

def tile_latencies(base, n=60):
    out = []
    with httpx.Client() as c:
        for t in (tiles14 * 3)[:n]:
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            c.get(f"{base}/tiles/ndvi/{t.z}/{t.x}/{t.y}.png")
            out.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
    return np.array(out)

def under_load(base):
    "Tile latencies alone and during a full-resolution download by another process."
    alone = tile_latencies(base)
    download = subprocess.Popen(["curl", "-s", "-o", "/dev/null", "-w", "%{size_download} %{time_total}",
                                 f"{base}/collections/unions/items?limit=10000"],
                                stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, text=True)
    time.sleep(0.1)
    busy = tile_latencies(base)
    size, seconds = download.communicate()[0].split()
    return alone, busy, int(size) / 1e6, float(seconds)

# 1) the server inside this notebook
inproc = web.start_server(web.create_app(
    rasters={"ndvi": {"path": ndvi_path, "colormap": "RdYlGn", "rescale": (-0.1, 0.9)}},
    vectors={"unions": unions_full}))                     # full resolution: 7.8 million vertices
results = {"in notebook, 1 process": under_load(inproc.url)}
inproc.stop()

# 2) the same app in a module, served by 4 uvicorn worker processes
app_code = "\n".join([
    "import geopandas as gpd",
    "import geolattice.web as web",
    f"unions = gpd.read_file(r'{(BD / 'Shapefiles' / 'bd_union_GCS.shp').resolve()}')[['ADM4_EN', 'ADM3_EN', 'ADM2_EN', 'geometry']]",
    f"app = web.create_app(rasters={{'ndvi': {{'path': r'{ndvi_path.resolve()}', 'colormap': 'RdYlGn', 'rescale': (-0.1, 0.9)}}}},",
    "                     vectors={'unions': unions})", ""])
(OUT / "unions_app.py").write_text(app_code)
with socket.socket() as sock:
    sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); port = sock.getsockname()[1]
workers = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-m", "uvicorn", "unions_app:app", "--port", str(port), "--workers", "4",
                            "--log-level", "warning"], cwd=OUT, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
base = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}"
time.sleep(3)
for _ in range(300):                                       # wait until the workers answer
    try:
        if http.get(base + "/collections/unions/items?limit=1").status_code == 200:
            break
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        pass
    time.sleep(0.5)
time.sleep(10)                                             # let every worker finish loading the data
results["uvicorn, 4 worker processes"] = under_load(base)
workers.terminate(); workers.wait()

rows = {}
for name, (alone, busy, mb_, s_) in results.items():
    rows[(name, "tiles alone")] = [np.median(alone), np.percentile(alone, 95), alone.max()]
    rows[(name, "during download")] = [np.median(busy), np.percentile(busy, 95), busy.max()]
    print(f"{name}: the download of {mb_:.0f} MB took {s_:.1f} s")
pd.DataFrame(rows, index=["median ms", "95th percentile ms", "max ms"]).round(1)

Downloading the full-resolution unions (301 MB) took about 3 s either way. The median tile time barely changed, but the tail did. With the server inside the notebook, the slowest tile waited 1.6 s while the download was being encoded: the encoding thread and the tile thread take turns on one interpreter lock. With four uvicorn worker processes, the tile requests were answered by other processes and the slowest took 115 ms. Each worker holds its own copy of the data, so memory grows with the number of workers.
Two fixes in create_app came out of this measurement. Feature responses used to be encoded on the event loop, three times over (to_json, json.loads, json.dumps); while one large request was being encoded, every other request waited; in our tests a 1,000-union page took 4.9 s. Features are now encoded once, with GEOS, in a worker thread that yields between chunks; the same page took about 0.7 s, and the server kept answering tiles meanwhile.

title: Serving Maps: Tiles and OGC APIs
section: Vector tiles as one file: PMTiles
text:
Vector tiles as one file: PMTiles
Vector tiles cut features into the XYZ grid, simplified for each zoom, and the browser styles them. A PMTiles archive stores a whole tile set in one file with an index at the front; a map reads the header, then fetches each tile with an HTTP range request. Any static host serves it: no tile server, no database. We write the unions as PMTiles, read the archive over HTTP with the pmtiles Python reader, and count the bytes.


Code
# Write unions to PMTiles and fetch individual tiles over HTTP range requests
t0 = time.perf_counter()
pm_path = write_pmtiles(OUT / "unions.pmtiles", unions[["ADM4_EN", "ADM3_EN", "ADM2_EN", "geometry"]],
                        layer="unions", minzoom=5, maxzoom=12)
print(f"unions.pmtiles: {Path(pm_path).stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB, written in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

def http_source(url, server):
    "pmtiles byte source over HTTP range requests."
    def get_bytes(offset, length):
        return http.get(url, headers={"Range": f"bytes={offset}-{offset + length - 1}"}).content
    return get_bytes

static.reset()
reader = pmr.Reader(http_source(f"{static.url}/unions.pmtiles", static))
header, meta = reader.header(), reader.metadata()
print(f"opened: {static.stats['requests']} requests, {static.stats['bytes'] / 1e3:.1f} kB")
print({k: header[k] for k in ("min_zoom", "max_zoom", "addressed_tiles_count", "tile_contents_count", "tile_compression")})
print("layers:", [l["id"] for l in meta.get("vector_layers", [])])

rows = []
for z in [6, 8, 10, 12]:
    t = web.lonlat_to_tile(90.40, 23.78, z)
    static.reset()
    data = reader.get(z, t.x, t.y)
    rows.append({"zoom": z, "tile": f"{z}/{t.x}/{t.y}", "tile kB": round(len(data) / 1e3, 1),
                 "requests": static.stats["requests"], "kB transferred": round(static.stats["bytes"] / 1e3, 1)})

The archive is 7.9 MB for all 5,160 unions at zooms 5-12, smaller than the 9.55 MB GeoJSON of the same simplified layer, and it carries every zoom level. Opening it cost 3 requests and 2.0 kB (the header, the root directory and the metadata). A tile then costs its own size plus a directory read: 263 kB for a whole-country tile at zoom 6, falling to 4.3 kB at zoom 12, where a tile covers a few unions. This simple reader fetches directories again for every tile, about 6 kB each time; the browser’s pmtiles library caches them.
A MapLibre page displays the archive with the pmtiles JavaScript protocol. The page and the file sit side by side on the static server, which is exactly how they would be published on S3 or GitHub Pages.

Checklist before a service goes public:

HTTPS and a stable domain; set cors to the sites that may use the service.
Caching: Cache-Control headers and a CDN in front of tiles; tiles are the same for every user.
Limits: a maximum page size (max_limit) and rate limiting, so one client cannot exhaust the server.
Data preparation: COGs with overviews, simplified geometry for display, spatial indexes.
Monitoring: request logs, latency percentiles and error rates.
Authentication when data are not public (API keys or OAuth in front of the service; Notebook 08_06).
Standards: check OGC conformance with the OGC test suite (TEAM Engine) before announcing an OGC API.

Notebook 08_06 builds custom APIs with FastAPI, which can mount a create_app service as one part (app.mount("/gis", create_app(...))); Notebook 08_10 packages services in Docker.

title: Serving Maps: Tiles and OGC APIs
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

XYZ tiles and TileJSON are the common language of web maps; OGC API: Features is the standard for feature access, with paging, bbox, attribute filters and datetime, described in OpenAPI.
Static pyramids are fastest and need no server, but grow fourfold per zoom; dynamic servers render from the source on request and need COGs with overviews to be efficient over the network.
A service is only useful if others’ clients work with it: test with GDAL, QGIS and OWSLib.
One process serves tiles and features together only if heavy requests do not block light ones.
PMTiles publishes vector tiles as one static file read with range requests.

What we measured

Static tiles: 3.0 ms median per tile, but 22.2 million tiles to cover Bangladesh to zoom 18.
Dynamic tiles: 34 ms median from a local file; zoomed-out tiles from a COG read 0.82 MB against 10.0 MB from a plain GeoTIFF.
The OGC API service answered bbox, attribute and datetime queries, and GDAL, GeoPandas and OWSLib read it unchanged.
During a 301 MB download, the slowest tile took 1.6 s with one process and 115 ms with four worker processes.
PMTiles: 7.9 MB for all unions and zooms 5-12; opening costs 2 kB, a zoom-12 tile 4.3 kB.
Fixes made to geolattice.web along the way:

/api and datetime;
timestamp encoding;
faster, non-blocking feature encoding;
overview reads in render_tile;
start-up checks of raster settings;
start_server;
static_server(subprocess=True).


Exercises

Add the July and September NDVI as two tile layers of one create_app and open /viewer. How many tiles does a full-screen view at zoom 13 request? (Watch the server log with log_level="info".)
Serve stack_none_1.tif (no compression) next to the COG and repeat the bytes-per-tile table.
Publish fields with a date column (assign a sampling date to each field) and query a month with datetime.
Use ogr2ogr (gdal.VectorTranslate) to copy only the Barisal unions from the service, using where and a spatial filter, and compare the transfer with the full layer.
Write the district poverty layer as PMTiles and style it as a choropleth in the MapLibre page with a step expression on poverty_pct.

References

OGC API, Features, Part 1: Core (OGC 17-069r4). https://docs.ogc.org/is/17-069r4/17-069r4.html
OGC Two Dimensional Tile Matrix Set and OGC API: Tiles. https://ogcapi.ogc.org/tiles/
TileJSON specification. https://github.com/mapbox/tilejson-spec
PMTiles specification. https://github.com/protomaps/PMTiles
Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF. https://cogeo.org
TiTiler, pygeoapi and Martin documentation. https://developmentseed.org/titiler/, https://pygeoapi.io, https://maplibre.org/martin/

title: Spatial SQL: DuckDB, GeoPackage and PostGIS
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Setup: imports, paths, output folder, and an in-memory DuckDB with the spatial extension
%matplotlib inline
import os
import shutil
import time
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)

import duckdb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import geolattice
import geolattice.web as web
from geolattice.vector import read_geoparquet, write_geoparquet

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})
DATA = Path("../../../Data")
BD = DATA / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "Bangladesh"
OUT = DATA / "00_shared" / "data_web_cloud_gis" / "08_03_outputs"
if OUT.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(OUT)
OUT.mkdir(parents=True)

# Connect and load DuckDB spatial; helpers return pandas / GeoDataFrames
con = duckdb.connect()                                   # an in-memory database
con.sql("INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial; SET enable_progress_bar = false;")
print("geolattice", geolattice.__version__, "| DuckDB", duckdb.__version__,
      "| spatial functions:", con.sql("SELECT count(DISTINCT function_name) FROM duckdb_functions() WHERE function_name LIKE 'ST_%'").fetchone()[0])

def q(sql):
    "Run SQL and return a pandas DataFrame."
    return con.sql(sql).df()

def to_gdf(sql, geom="geom", crs=4326):
    "Run SQL whose result has a geometry column and return a GeoDataFrame (geometry travels as WKB)."
    df = con.sql(f"SELECT * EXCLUDE ({geom}), ST_AsWKB({geom}) AS __wkb FROM ({sql})").df()
    geometry = gpd.GeoSeries.from_wkb(df.pop("__wkb").map(bytes), crs=crs)
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(df, geometry=geometry.values, crs=crs).rename_geometry(geom)

Spatial functions and the axis-order trap
A first query uses several functions at once: validity, geometry type, vertex count, area on the ellipsoid and the centroid.

For metric work (buffers, distances, areas) data are usually projected. Here is the trap: EPSG:4326 officially lists latitude first. DuckDB’s ST_Transform follows the official axis order unless told otherwise, so a point stored as (longitude, latitude) is read the wrong way round.


Code
# Compare ST_Transform axis order with and without always_xy := true
q('''
SELECT ST_AsText(ST_Transform(ST_Point(90.40, 23.81), 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:32646'))                       AS default_order,
       ST_AsText(ST_Transform(ST_Point(90.40, 23.81), 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:32646', always_xy := true))   AS always_xy,
       ST_AsText(ST_Transform(ST_Point(23.81, 90.40), 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:32646'))                       AS lat_lon_input''')

0

POINT (235102.69622060267 2635618.6821711794)







The first column is the trap: transforming ST_Point(90.40, 23.81) from EPSG:4326 with the default settings gives POINT (inf inf), because DuckDB read 90.40 as a latitude, which is impossible. Supplying the coordinates as (latitude, longitude), or adding always_xy := true, gives the correct UTM position (about 235 km east, 2,636 km north). Coordinates in files are almost always stored longitude first, so use always_xy := true whenever the source is EPSG:4326.
The query above it also shows why projected or ellipsoidal measures matter: the largest upazilas are in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (Baghai Chhari, 1,616 km²) and the Sundarbans coast (Shyamnagar, Mongla, Koyra). The coastal ones are multipolygons with over 10,000 vertices each, because of their many islands and channels.

text:
Attribute joins and join quality
The poverty table has one row per upazila with an upazila code (ADM3_PCODE), so joining it to the upazila polygons should give a poverty map. Before trusting any join, check three numbers: how many rows match, how many rows are left over on each side (anti-joins), and whether the key is unique.


Code
# Check how well poverty rows join to upazila polygons on ADM3_PCODE
q('''
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM upazila)                                            AS polygons,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM poverty)                                            AS poverty_rows,
       (SELECT count(DISTINCT ADM3_PCODE) FROM poverty)                          AS distinct_codes_in_table,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM upazila u JOIN poverty p USING (ADM3_PCODE))        AS joined_rows,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM upazila u ANTI JOIN poverty p USING (ADM3_PCODE))   AS polygons_without_data''')

The numbers do not add up. 544 rows joined, yet 19 polygons got no data, and the table has only 525 distinct codes for 544 rows. Sixteen codes are repeated, and the repeats carry different poverty values: BD303334 appears four times (15.7, 24.0, 35.3 and 48.0%), once for each upazila called Kaliganj in four districts.
Whoever built the table assigned codes by upazila name, so upazilas sharing a name received the same code. A plain join therefore attaches four different poverty rates to Gazipur’s Kaliganj and none to the other three. Here the row count looked right, which makes this the most dangerous kind of join error. Checking count(DISTINCT key) catches it.
The fix is a key that really identifies an upazila: the district code plus the upazila name. bd_data.csv holds the same poverty values with district codes and names. Names still differ in spelling, so we join in three steps and record how each row was matched:

exact match on district code and lower-case name;
fuzzy match for the rest: same district (by code, or by a near-identical district name), names normalised (spaces, punctuation, “Upazila” and bracketed parts removed), best Jaro-Winkler similarity of at least 0.9;
a small manual lookup for names that changed, which no string similarity can find.



Code
# Build poverty_clean: exact name match, then fuzzy match, then a few manual fixes
con.sql(r'''CREATE MACRO norm(s) AS
    regexp_replace(regexp_replace(lower(trim(s)), '\s*upazila$|\s*\(.*\)', '', 'g'), '[^a-z]', '', 'g')''')
con.sql("CREATE TABLE manual_names (district VARCHAR, upazila VARCHAR, table_district VARCHAR, table_upazila VARCHAR, reason VARCHAR)")
con.sql('''INSERT INTO manual_names VALUES
    ('Jessore',   'Kotwali',         'Jessore',          'Jessore Sadar',          'Kotwali is the Jessore Sadar upazila'),
    ('Nawabganj', 'Nawabganj Sadar', 'Chapai Nababganj', 'Chapai Nababganj Sadar', 'Nawabganj district was renamed Chapai Nawabganj')''')
con.sql('''
CREATE TABLE poverty_clean AS
WITH exact AS (
    SELECT u.ADM3_PCODE, b.POVERTY_PERCENT AS poverty, 'exact' AS matched_by
    FROM upazila u JOIN bd_data b ON u.ADM2_PCODE = b.DISTRICT_PCODE AND lower(trim(u.ADM3_EN)) = lower(trim(b.UPAZILA_NAME))),
rest_u AS (SELECT * FROM upazila WHERE ADM3_PCODE NOT IN (SELECT ADM3_PCODE FROM exact)),
rest_b AS (SELECT * FROM bd_data b WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM upazila u WHERE u.ADM2_PCODE = b.DISTRICT_PCODE AND lower(trim(u.ADM3_EN)) = lower(trim(b.UPAZILA_NAME)))),
fuzzy AS (
    SELECT ADM3_PCODE, poverty, 'fuzzy' AS matched_by FROM (
        SELECT u.ADM3_PCODE, b.POVERTY_PERCENT AS poverty,
               jaro_winkler_similarity(norm(u.ADM3_EN), norm(b.UPAZILA_NAME)) AS sim,
               row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY u.ADM3_PCODE
                                  ORDER BY jaro_winkler_similarity(norm(u.ADM3_EN), norm(b.UPAZILA_NAME)) DESC) AS r
        FROM rest_u u JOIN rest_b b
          ON u.ADM2_PCODE = b.DISTRICT_PCODE OR jaro_winkler_similarity(norm(u.ADM2_EN), norm(b.DISTRICT_NAME)) > 0.9)
    WHERE r = 1 AND sim >= 0.9),
manual AS (
    SELECT u.ADM3_PCODE, b.POVERTY_PERCENT AS poverty, 'manual' AS matched_by
    FROM manual_names m
    JOIN upazila u ON u.ADM2_EN = m.district AND u.ADM3_EN = m.upazila
    JOIN bd_data b ON b.DISTRICT_NAME = m.table_district AND b.UPAZILA_NAME = m.table_upazila)
SELECT * FROM exact UNION ALL SELECT * FROM fuzzy UNION ALL SELECT * FROM manual''')
q('''SELECT matched_by, count(*) AS upazilas FROM poverty_clean GROUP BY 1
     UNION ALL SELECT 'total distinct codes', count(DISTINCT ADM3_PCODE) FROM poverty_clean
     UNION ALL SELECT 'polygons still without data', (SELECT count(*) FROM upazila u ANTI JOIN poverty_clean USING (ADM3_PCODE))''')

# Fuzzy-match population from the indicators table onto upazila polygons by name
con.sql('''
CREATE TABLE pop_clean AS
SELECT ADM3_PCODE, population, sim FROM (
    SELECT u.ADM3_PCODE, i."Total Population (N)" AS population,
           jaro_winkler_similarity(norm(u.ADM3_EN), norm(i."Upazila Name")) AS sim,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY u.ADM3_PCODE
                              ORDER BY jaro_winkler_similarity(norm(u.ADM3_EN), norm(i."Upazila Name")) DESC) AS r
    FROM upazila u JOIN indicators i ON jaro_winkler_similarity(norm(u.ADM2_EN), norm(i."Zila Name")) > 0.9)
WHERE r = 1 AND sim >= 0.9''')
q('''SELECT count(*) AS upazilas_with_population, count(*) FILTER (WHERE sim < 1) AS fuzzy_matches,
            (SELECT count(*) FROM upazila) - count(*) AS without_population,
            sum(population) AS total_population FROM pop_clean''')

The three-step join links every upazila exactly once:

521 exact matches on district code and name;
21 fuzzy matches. Most are spelling variants (“Daulatkhan” / “Daulat Khan”, “Tungi Para” / “Tungipara”); nine are all upazilas of one district, spelled “Brahamanbaria” in the shapefile and “Brahmanbaria”, with a different district code, in the table;
2 manual matches for places whose names changed. No string similarity links “Kotwali” to “Jessore Sadar”, or “Nawabganj” to “Chapai Nababganj”.

The population table matched 538 upazilas (3 fuzzy). The 6 without population drop out of the population weights in the next section.
The original code-only join was not just incomplete but wrong. It also inflates aggregates: the duplicated rows would add extra “upazilas” to districts such as Bogra, Rangpur and Netrakona (Exercise 2).

title: Spatial SQL: DuckDB, GeoPackage and PostGIS
section: Dissolve and aggregate: from upazilas to districts
text:
Dissolve and aggregate: from upazilas to districts
ST_Union_Agg merges the polygons of each group (a dissolve). Combined with GROUP BY and the joined tables we build district statistics in one query: area, population, population-weighted poverty and rice production from the district table.


Code
# Dissolve upazilas to districts, then join rice production into district_stats
t0 = time.perf_counter()
con.sql('''
CREATE TABLE districts AS
WITH u AS (
    SELECT z.ADM1_EN, z.ADM2_EN, z.ADM2_PCODE, z.geom, pv.poverty, p.population
    FROM upazila z
    LEFT JOIN poverty_clean pv USING (ADM3_PCODE)
    LEFT JOIN pop_clean p USING (ADM3_PCODE))
SELECT ADM1_EN AS division, ADM2_EN AS district, ADM2_PCODE,
       count(*) AS upazilas,
       ST_Union_Agg(geom) AS geom,
       CAST(sum(population) AS BIGINT) AS population,
       CAST(round(sum(poverty * population) / sum(population) FILTER (WHERE poverty IS NOT NULL), 1) AS DOUBLE) AS poverty_pct
FROM u GROUP BY ALL''')
con.sql('''
CREATE TABLE district_stats AS
SELECT d.*, CAST(round(ST_Area_Spheroid(ST_FlipCoordinates(d.geom)) / 1e6) AS DOUBLE) AS area_km2,
       CAST(r.Aus + r.Aman + r.Boro AS BIGINT) AS rice_t,
       CAST(round(100.0 * r.Boro / (r.Aus + r.Aman + r.Boro), 1) AS DOUBLE) AS boro_share_pct
FROM districts d LEFT JOIN rice r USING (ADM2_PCODE)''')
print(f"Dissolved 544 upazilas into {q('SELECT count(*) n FROM districts').n[0]} districts in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
q('''SELECT division, district, upazilas, area_km2, population, poverty_pct, rice_t, boro_share_pct,
            round(rice_t / area_km2) AS rice_t_per_km2
     FROM district_stats ORDER BY rice_t DESC LIMIT 8''')

One query dissolved 544 upazilas into 64 district polygons in about a second, and attached population, population-weighted poverty and rice production. The largest producer was Mymensingh (1.71 million t in 2018-19), followed by Dinajpur and Naogaon. Boro, the irrigated dry-season crop, made up 46-71% of production in these leading districts. Production density ranges from close to zero in the Chittagong Hill Tracts to about 500 t per km² in the north-west.
The poverty map shows the familiar geography: highest in the far north (Kurigram) and along the Padma-Meghna river belt, lowest around Dhaka and in the central-west.

section: Spatial joins: arsenic in rice fields
text:
Spatial joins: arsenic in rice fields
A spatial join matches rows by geometry instead of by key. Each of the 263 sampled rice fields is assigned to the union that contains it, and the water, soil and grain arsenic are summarised per union. The World Health Organization guideline for arsenic in drinking water is 0.01 mg/L and the Bangladesh standard is 0.05 mg/L; irrigation water above these levels moves arsenic into soil and rice.

       string_agg(DISTINCT u.ADM3_EN, ', ') AS upazila_names,
       string_agg(DISTINCT u.ADM2_EN, ', ') AS districts
FROM fields f LEFT JOIN unions u ON ST_Within(f.geom, u.geom)''')

All 263 fields fall inside a union: 12 unions of Tala upazila, Satkhira district, in the south-west. Arsenic in the irrigation water is high everywhere:

the union means range from 0.051 mg/L (Tala union) to 0.198 mg/L (Magura union);
in every union except Tala itself, at least 45% of fields exceed the Bangladesh drinking-water standard of 0.05 mg/L;
every union has fields above the WHO guideline of 0.01 mg/L.

text:
Distance queries and window functions
Distances need a projected coordinate system (metres). We project to UTM zone 46N (with always_xy := true) and ask: how many unions lie within 5 km of at least one sampled field? Then a window function ranks upazilas by poverty within each division, a task that would need a loop in plain Python.

# Count unions within 5 km of any field after projecting both layers to UTM 46N
q('''
WITH f AS (SELECT ST_Transform(geom, 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:32646', always_xy := true) AS g FROM fields),
     u AS (SELECT ADM4_EN, ADM3_EN, ST_Transform(geom, 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:32646', always_xy := true) AS g
           FROM unions WHERE ST_Intersects(geom, (SELECT ST_Buffer(ST_Envelope(ST_Collect(list(geom))), 0.2) FROM fields)))
SELECT count(DISTINCT u.ADM4_EN) AS unions_within_5_km, count(DISTINCT u.ADM3_EN) AS upazilas,
       round(max(ST_Distance(u.g, f.g)) / 1000, 2) AS max_km_checked
FROM u JOIN f ON ST_DWithin(u.g, f.g, 5000)''')

title: Spatial SQL: DuckDB, GeoPackage and PostGIS
text:
Spatial indexes: when they help
A spatial index (an R-tree) stores bounding boxes in a tree so a query can skip features far from the area of interest. DuckDB already builds a temporary index inside a spatial join, so an explicit index matters mostly for repeated selective queries against a stored table. We time both cases on 200,000 random points.


Code
# Benchmark spatial joins with and without an R-tree index on 200k random points
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200_000
con.register("pts_df", pd.DataFrame({"lon": rng.uniform(88.0, 92.7, n), "lat": rng.uniform(20.6, 26.6, n)}))
con.sql("CREATE TABLE points AS SELECT row_number() OVER () AS id, ST_Point(lon, lat) AS geom FROM pts_df")

def timed(sql, repeat=1):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeat):
        result = con.sql(sql).fetchone()[0]
    return result, (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeat

join_sql = "SELECT count(*) FROM points p JOIN unions u ON ST_Contains(u.geom, p.geom)"
window_sql = "SELECT count(*) FROM points WHERE ST_Intersects(geom, ST_MakeEnvelope(90.35, 23.70, 90.45, 23.82))"
plan = con.sql("EXPLAIN " + join_sql).fetchall()[0][1]
print("The join is planned as:", [l.strip(" │") for l in plan.split("\n") if "JOIN" in l][0])
rows = []
n_join, t_join = timed(join_sql)
n_win, t_win = timed(window_sql, repeat=20)
rows += [{"query": "points in unions (spatial join)", "index": "none", "result": n_join, "seconds": t_join},
         {"query": "points in a Dhaka box (×20, average)", "index": "none", "result": n_win, "seconds": t_win}]
# Build R-tree and repeat the same queries for a before/after timing table
t0 = time.perf_counter()
con.sql("CREATE INDEX points_rtree ON points USING RTREE (geom)")
t_build = time.perf_counter() - t0
n_join2, t_join2 = timed(join_sql)
n_win2, t_win2 = timed(window_sql, repeat=20)
rows += [{"query": "points in unions (spatial join)", "index": "R-tree on points", "result": n_join2, "seconds": t_join2},
         {"query": "points in a Dhaka box (×20, average)", "index": "R-tree on points", "result": n_win2, "seconds": t_win2}]
print(f"R-tree built in {t_build:.2f} s")

DuckDB planned the 200,000-point join as a SPATIAL_JOIN, which builds its own temporary index, so an explicit R-tree changed nothing (about 1.35 s both ways). For the selective query, points inside a small Dhaka box repeated 20 times, the R-tree (built in 0.04 s) made each query 25-30 times faster (about 0.016 s down to under 0.001 s), because the index finds the 69 matching points without scanning all 200,000.
Indexes cost time to build and space to store. They pay off for tables that are queried repeatedly with small windows, which is typical of web services.

title: Spatial SQL: DuckDB, GeoPackage and PostGIS
section: From SQL to GeoPandas and to files
text:
From SQL to GeoPandas and to files
Results move to GeoPandas through WKB (Section 6 used the small to_gdf helper). DuckDB also writes files directly with COPY: Parquet with GeoParquet metadata, and any GDAL format.


Code
# Export district_stats to Parquet, GeoPackage, FlatGeobuf, and GeoParquet
src = "SELECT district, division, population, poverty_pct, rice_t, area_km2, geom FROM district_stats"
con.sql(f"COPY ({src}) TO '{(OUT / 'districts_duckdb.parquet').as_posix()}' (FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION zstd)")
con.sql(f"COPY ({src}) TO '{(OUT / 'districts.gpkg').as_posix()}' WITH (FORMAT GDAL, DRIVER 'GPKG', SRS 'EPSG:4326')")
con.sql(f"COPY ({src}) TO '{(OUT / 'districts.fgb').as_posix()}' WITH (FORMAT GDAL, DRIVER 'FlatGeobuf', SRS 'EPSG:4326')")
write_geoparquet(OUT / "districts_geolattice.parquet", dist.merge(q("SELECT district, population FROM district_stats"), on="district"))
rows = []
for name in ["districts_duckdb.parquet", "districts_geolattice.parquet"]:
    i = web.geoparquet_info(OUT / name)
    rows.append({"file": name, "GeoParquet version": i["version"], "bbox covering": i["covering"],
                 "CRS": i["crs"].to_string() if i["crs"] is not None else None, "rows": i["num_rows"],
                 "KB": round((OUT / name).stat().st_size / 1e3)})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))
print("GeoPackage and FlatGeobuf read back:", len(gpd.read_file(OUT / "districts.gpkg")), len(gpd.read_file(OUT / "districts.fgb")))

Large integer sums become 38-digit DECIMAL values in DuckDB, which GDAL cannot store. This is why the district query casts population and production to BIGINT.

title: Spatial SQL: DuckDB, GeoPackage and PostGIS
section: A GeoPackage is a SQLite database
text:
A GeoPackage is a SQLite database
A GeoPackage file is an SQLite database with standard tables for metadata and an R-tree spatial index per layer. GDAL can run SQL against it in the SQLite dialect, including spatial functions, and the R-tree can be queried like any table.


Code
# Query the GeoPackage with SQLite spatial SQL via its built-in R-tree
from osgeo import gdal, ogr
gdal.UseExceptions()
gpkg = gdal.OpenEx((OUT / "districts.gpkg").as_posix(), gdal.OF_VECTOR)
layer_name = gpkg.GetLayer(0).GetName()
print("Layer:", layer_name)
system = gpkg.ExecuteSQL("SELECT table_name, data_type FROM gpkg_contents UNION ALL "
                         "SELECT table_name, extension_name FROM gpkg_extensions", dialect="SQLite")
print([tuple(f.GetField(i) for i in range(2)) for f in system]); gpkg.ReleaseResultSet(system)

sql = f'''SELECT district, poverty_pct, ST_Area(geom) AS area_deg2
          FROM "{layer_name}"
          WHERE fid IN (SELECT id FROM "rtree_{layer_name}_geom"
                        WHERE minx <= 90.45 AND maxx >= 90.35 AND miny <= 23.82 AND maxy >= 23.70)'''
result = gpkg.ExecuteSQL(sql, dialect="SQLite")
print("Districts whose R-tree box overlaps central Dhaka:",
      [(f.GetField("district"), f.GetField("poverty_pct")) for f in result])
gpkg.ReleaseResultSet(result); gpkg = None


Layer: districts
[('districts', 'features'), ('districts', 'gpkg_rtree_index')]
Districts whose R-tree box overlaps central Dhaka: [('Narayanganj', 26.1), ('Dhaka', 15.3)]


The R-tree table (rtree_<layer>_geom) holds one bounding box per feature; filtering it first is exactly what a spatial index does. The same file opens in QGIS, ArcGIS and any SQLite client.

title: Spatial SQL: DuckDB, GeoPackage and PostGIS
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Spatial SQL expresses joins, dissolves, filters and rankings declaratively, and runs them where the data live; DuckDB brings it to files with no server.
Always check joins: row counts, anti-joins and key uniqueness. A duplicated key silently multiplies rows; name-based joins need normalisation, fuzzy matching and sometimes a manual lookup.
ST_Transform from EPSG:4326 needs always_xy := true in DuckDB when coordinates are stored lon/lat.
Spatial joins build their own index; explicit R-tree indexes pay off for repeated selective queries.
GeoPackage is SQLite; PostGIS is the multi-user server; cloud warehouses speak the same ST_ language.

What we found

The upazila poverty table had duplicated codes, assigned by name, that a plain join would have attached to the wrong places. Rebuilding the key (district code plus name, then fuzzy and manual matching) linked all 544 upazilas.
One SQL query dissolved upazilas to 64 districts with population-weighted poverty and rice production.
All 263 arsenic-sampled rice fields lie in 12 unions of Tala upazila. Mean irrigation-water arsenic is 0.05-0.20 mg/L, mostly above the national standard.
An R-tree index made a repeated window query 25-30 times faster, but did not speed up a spatial join, which builds its own index.

Exercises

Join poverty_clean to the union layer through the upazila code (ADM3_PCODE) and map poverty at union level. Why does every union in an upazila get the same value?
Redo the district statistics with the original bd_poverty.csv join (duplicated codes included). Which districts change most, and why?
Use ST_Read and read_parquet over HTTP (Notebook 08_02’s static_server and the httpfs extension) to run the Section 7 spatial join against the remote unions.parquet.
Compute, for each division, the share of its area that lies within 10 km of a district boundary.
If you can run PostGIS (Docker), set GEOLATTICE_POSTGIS, load the union layer with ogr2ogr, add a GiST index and compare the spatial-join time with DuckDB.

References

DuckDB spatial extension. https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/spatial
PostGIS documentation. https://postgis.net/documentation
Obe, R. & Hsu, L. (2021). PostGIS in Action, 3rd ed. Manning.
GeoPackage encoding standard (OGC 12-128r19). https://www.geopackage.org
WHO (2022). Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, 4th ed. incorporating the first and second addenda (arsenic 0.01 mg/L).

text:
Getting imagery with get_images
We want the clearest Sentinel-2 scene of each summer month. search_images lists candidates without downloading; we keep scenes from MGRS tile 18TVN, which covers the whole area, so all dates share one pixel grid, and pick the least cloudy scene per month. get_images(search=..., ids=...) then downloads only those scenes, clipped to the area (mode="clip", the default), with the red, green, blue, NIR and scene-classification (scl) bands and an RGB+NIR stack.tif.
The download runs once; later runs (and later notebooks) reuse the folder.


Code
# Search for clear Sentinel-2 scenes on tile 18TVN and download if needed
S2_DIR = WORK / "s2_syracuse_2025"
found = search_images(bbox=AOI, dates=("2025-06-01", "2025-09-30"), source="earth-search",
                      collection="sentinel-2-l2a", cloud=20, limit=500, quiet=True)
cands = pd.DataFrame(found.scenes)
cands["date"] = pd.to_datetime(cands["datetime"])
cands = cands[cands["id"].str.contains("18TVN")]
best = cands.sort_values("cloud").groupby(cands["date"].dt.month).head(1).sort_values("date")

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
text:
Is it cloud-optimized?
validate_cog checks the layout rules of a COG:

tiled pixels (square blocks, not full-width strips);
internal overviews for images larger than about 512 pixels;
headers first: the image file directories (IFDs) at the start, full resolution then overviews;
data ordered from the smallest overview to full resolution, after all headers.

Missing overviews and a missing LAYOUT=COG marker are warnings; strict=True treats them as errors.


Code
# Validate that the local multi-band stack is a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF
stack_path = S2_DIR / SCENES[0] / "stack.tif"
report = web.validate_cog(stack_path)
print(report)
pd.Series({k: report.details[k] for k in ["size", "bands", "dtype", "block_size", "overview_count", "compression", "layout"]}).to_frame("value")

The file get_images wrote is a tiled (256 × 256), DEFLATE-compressed GeoTIFF, which is fine for local work, but it is not a COG. It has no overviews, and GDAL’s ordinary GeoTIFF writer put the pixel data before the image file directories, so a remote reader would have to look for the headers. The source it was clipped from, the Sentinel-2 band on AWS, is a valid COG: 1,024-pixel blocks, four overviews and the LAYOUT=COG marker. Clipping keeps the pixels but not the layout, which is why outputs should be converted before they are published.

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
section: Converting to COG and choosing compression
text:
Converting to COG and choosing compression
to_cog uses GDAL’s COG driver, which tiles the image, builds internal overviews and writes the parts in the right order. The main choices are compression and, for integer data, the predictor: predictor 2 stores the difference between neighbouring pixels, which are small for smooth imagery and compress better. All the options below are lossless.


Code
# Rewrite the stack as COGs under several compression options and compare size/speed
options = {
    "none":               dict(compress="NONE"),
    "LZW":                dict(compress="LZW"),
    "DEFLATE":            dict(compress="DEFLATE"),
    "DEFLATE + predictor": dict(compress="DEFLATE", predictor=2),
    "ZSTD + predictor":   dict(compress="ZSTD", predictor=2),
    "ZSTD level 15 + predictor": dict(compress="ZSTD", predictor=2, level=15),
}
# Uncompressed reference array for lossless checks
with rasterio.open(stack_path) as src:
    reference = src.read()
rows = []
# Write each variant, time readback, and record COG details
for name, opts in options.items():
    dst = OUT / f"stack_{name.split()[0].lower()}_{len(opts)}.tif"
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); web.to_cog(stack_path, dst, blocksize=512, **opts); t_write = time.perf_counter() - t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with rasterio.open(dst) as src:
        back = src.read()
    t_read = time.perf_counter() - t0
    rep = web.validate_cog(dst, strict=True)
    rows.append({"option": name, "MB": dst.stat().st_size / 1e6, "write s": t_write, "read s": t_read,
                 "lossless": bool(np.array_equal(back, reference)), "strict COG": rep.valid,
                 "overviews": rep.details["overview_count"]})
comp = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("option")
comp["vs. input"] = (comp["MB"] / (stack_path.stat().st_size / 1e6)).round(2)
print(f"Input stack.tif: {stack_path.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB ({reference.nbytes / 1e6:.1f} MB uncompressed in memory)")
comp.round(3)

Every option is lossless (the pixels read back unchanged) and, apart from the uncompressed file, passes the strict COG check. Each file includes two overview levels, which is why even the uncompressed COG (29.4 MB) is larger than the 16.1 MB of pixels.

The predictor helps: DEFLATE goes from 17.2 to 15.9 MB with predictor 2.

LZW, the old default, was the largest of the compressed files. A good general choice is ZSTD or DEFLATE with a predictor at the default level.

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
text:
Inside a COG
The DEFLATE + predictor file is our working COG. Its byte offsets show the layout rules at work, and its overviews are ready-made reduced copies.


Code
# Show COG overview layout and visualize RGB at each resolution level
cog_path = OUT / "stack_deflate_2.tif"
rep = web.validate_cog(cog_path)
layout = pd.DataFrame({
    "level": ["full resolution"] + [f"overview {i + 1}" for i in range(rep.details["overview_count"])],
    "size (px)": [rep.details["size"]] + rep.details["overview_sizes"],
    "IFD offset (byte)": rep.details["ifd_offsets"],
    "first tile offset (byte)": rep.details["data_offsets"],
})
display(layout)

# Render full resolution plus each overview
with rasterio.open(cog_path) as src:
    levels = [None] + list(range(len(src.overviews(1))))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(levels), figsize=(4.2 * len(levels), 4))
for ax, lvl in zip(axes, levels):
    with rasterio.open(cog_path, overview_level=lvl) if lvl is not None else rasterio.open(cog_path) as src:
        rgb = src.read([1, 2, 3]).astype("float32")
    p2, p98 = np.percentile(rgb, [2, 98])
    ax.imshow(np.clip((np.moveaxis(rgb, 0, -1) - p2) / (p98 - p2), 0, 1))
    ax.set_title(f"{'full' if lvl is None else f'overview {lvl + 1}'}: {rgb.shape[2]} × {rgb.shape[1]}")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
text:
Web-optimized COGs
A web map asks for tiles in Web Mercator. If the COG is already in Web Mercator and its blocks line up with the XYZ tile grid, a tile server can return blocks almost directly instead of reprojecting. to_cog(..., web_optimized=True) produces such a file.


Code
# Build a web-optimized COG aligned to the Web Mercator tile grid
web_cog = web.to_cog(cog_path, OUT / "stack_web_optimized.tif", web_optimized=True, predictor=2,
                     overview_resampling="AVERAGE", resampling="BILINEAR")
with rasterio.open(web_cog) as src:
    res = src.res[0]
    t = src.transform
    zoom = int(round(np.log2(2 * web.tiles.ORIGIN_SHIFT / (256 * res))))
    tile_span = 256 * res
    aligned = all(abs(((v + web.tiles.ORIGIN_SHIFT) / tile_span) - round((v + web.tiles.ORIGIN_SHIFT) / tile_span)) < 1e-6
                  for v in (t.c, web.tiles.ORIGIN_SHIFT - t.f))
    print(f"CRS {src.crs}, pixel {res:.3f} m (zoom {zoom}: {web.tile_resolution(zoom):.3f} m), "
          f"blocks {src.block_shapes[0]}, size {src.width} × {src.height}, {Path(web_cog).stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB")
    print(f"Upper-left corner on the zoom-{zoom} tile grid: {aligned}")
print(web.validate_cog(web_cog, strict=True))


CRS EPSG:3857, pixel 19.109 m (zoom 13: 19.109 m), blocks (512, 512), size 1536 × 1536, 8.3 MB
Upper-left corner on the zoom-13 tile grid: True
../../../data/data_web_cloud_gis/08_01_outputs/stack_web_optimized.tif: valid Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF


The web-optimized copy is in Web Mercator at 19.109 m per pixel, exactly the pixel size of XYZ zoom 13. Its corner falls on the zoom-13 tile grid, and its 512-pixel blocks are whole multiples of 256-pixel tiles, so map tiles at zoom 13 and below line up with blocks and overviews.
Two costs: the image was resampled from 10 m to 19 m (GDAL picks the nearest zoom level at or below the native resolution), and in Web Mercator the pixels are not equal-area. Keep the UTM COG for analysis and the web-optimized copy for display.

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
section: Local copy versus the cloud original
text:
Local copy versus the cloud original
get_images reads the area out of each remote COG with range requests. Reading the same window again straight from the cloud should give identical pixels.


Code
# Compare a local red band to the same window read from the remote COG
local = rs.read(S2_DIR / SCENES[1] / "red.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)
item1 = json.loads((S2_DIR / SCENES[1] / "item.json").read_text())
t0 = time.perf_counter()
with web.cloud_env(anonymous=True):
    remote_red = rs.read(item1["assets"]["red"]["href"], chunks={"x": 1024, "y": 1024}) \
        .squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.clip_box(*local.rio.bounds()).compute()
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
same_grid = remote_red.shape == local.shape and np.allclose(remote_red.x, local.x) and np.allclose(remote_red.y, local.y)
print(f"Remote clip {remote_red.shape} read in {elapsed:.1f} s; same grid: {same_grid}; "
      f"identical values: {bool(np.array_equal(remote_red.values, local.values, equal_nan=True))}")

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
section: From files to a data cube: scale, offset and cloud masks
text:
From files to a data cube: scale, offset and cloud masks
The three dates share one grid, so they stack into a cube with dimensions (time, y, x). The STAC item says reflectance = DN × scale + offset, with 0.0001 and −0.1. But read the metadata carefully: since processing baseline 04.00 (January 2022) ESA adds 1,000 to every Sentinel-2 L2A value, which the −0.1 offset removes, and Earth Search already removed it when it converted the data to COGs. The item flags this with earthsearch:boa_offset_applied: true, while raster:bands still lists the offset. Applying both would subtract it twice.
We can check this against Planetary Computer, which keeps ESA’s original values, by reading the same scene and window from both catalogues:


Code
# Optional: compare Earth Search vs Planetary Computer DN values for the same scene
item_aug = json.loads((S2_DIR / SCENES[1] / "item.json").read_text())
es_red = rs.read(S2_DIR / SCENES[1] / "red.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)
try:
    pc_items = rs.access.stac_search("sentinel-2-l2a", aoi=AOI, dates=(item_aug["properties"]["datetime"][:10],) * 2)
    pc_item = next(it for it in pc_items if "T18TVN" in it.id)
    pc_red = rs.read(pc_item.assets["B04"].href, chunks={"x": 1024, "y": 1024}).squeeze("band", drop=True) \
        .rio.clip_box(*es_red.rio.bounds()).compute()
    diff = (pc_red - es_red).values
    print(f"Planetary Computer {pc_item.id}\n  PC − Earth Search DN: median {np.nanmedian(diff):.0f}, "
          f"range {np.nanmin(diff):.0f} to {np.nanmax(diff):.0f}; "
          f"median red DN: PC {float(pc_red.median()):.0f}, Earth Search {float(es_red.median()):.0f}")
except Exception as exc:
    print("Planetary Computer not reachable, skipped:", type(exc).__name__)
print("earthsearch:boa_offset_applied =", item_aug["properties"].get("earthsearch:boa_offset_applied"))


Planetary Computer S2C_MSIL2A_20250802T154951_R054_T18TVN_20250802T212214
  PC − Earth Search DN: median 1000, range 1000 to 1000; median red DN: PC 1662, Earth Search 662
earthsearch:boa_offset_applied = True


For the same scene, every pixel on Planetary Computer is exactly 1,000 higher than on Earth Search (median red 1,662 against 662), and the Earth Search item reports earthsearch:boa_offset_applied = True. So for Earth Search the correct conversion is DN × 0.0001, with no further offset. Applying the −0.1 offset as well would make the red reflectance about −0.03 and NDVI meaningless (an earlier draft of this notebook did exactly that). When a dataset is available from more than one provider, check which conventions each one uses.
The scene classification is at 20 m and must be resampled to 10 m with nearest-neighbour before it can mask clouds (classes 3 cloud shadow, 8-9 cloud, 10 cirrus).


Code
# Build a multi-date reflectance cube, cloud mask, and NDVI for all scenes
BANDS = ["red", "green", "blue", "nir"]
CLOUDY = [3, 8, 9, 10]
layers = []
# Scale each band to reflectance and flag clear (non-cloudy) pixels
for sid in SCENES:
    meta = json.loads((S2_DIR / sid / "item.json").read_text())
    when = pd.Timestamp(meta["properties"]["datetime"]).tz_convert(None)
    bands = {}
    for b in BANDS:
        rb = meta["assets"][b]["raster:bands"][0]
        offset = 0.0 if meta["properties"].get("earthsearch:boa_offset_applied") else rb.get("offset", 0.0)
        da = rs.read(S2_DIR / sid / f"{b}.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)
        bands[b] = (da * rb.get("scale", 1.0) + offset).astype("float32")
    scl = rs.read(S2_DIR / sid / "scl.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
    scl = scl.rio.reproject_match(bands["red"], resampling=rasterio.enums.Resampling.nearest)
    ds = xr.Dataset(bands)
    ds["clear"] = ~scl.isin(CLOUDY) & (scl > 0)
    layers.append(ds.expand_dims(time=[when]))
# Concatenate along time and compute cloud-masked NDVI
cube = xr.concat(layers, dim="time").rio.write_crs(layers[0].rio.crs)
cube["ndvi"] = ((cube.nir - cube.red) / (cube.nir + cube.red)).where(cube.clear)
cube = cube.drop_vars("spatial_ref", errors="ignore").rio.write_crs(layers[0].rio.crs)
for v in cube.data_vars:                     # drop scale/offset attributes inherited from the files
    cube[v].attrs, cube[v].encoding = {}, {}
print(cube)
pd.DataFrame({"clear (%)": (cube.clear.mean(["x", "y"]) * 100).round(1).to_series(),
              "median NDVI": cube.ndvi.median(["x", "y"]).round(3).to_series(),
              "median red reflectance": cube.red.median(["x", "y"]).round(4).to_series()})

The scene classification marked 3.4% of the 23 July scene as cloud or shadow: the cumulus clouds in the south-east and their shadows, now holes in the NDVI map. August and September were fully clear.
Onondaga Lake is negative in July (about −0.09) and September (about −0.2), but slightly positive on 2 August (about +0.06). Water is normally negative, so on that date the lake was more reflective in the NIR, which would fit greenish water (for example an algal bloom) or thin haze. A single scene cannot tell which. title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
text:
Zarr data cubes
GeoTIFF stores one raster per file; a Zarr store holds an n-dimensional array cut into compressed chunks, one object per chunk, so a cube of any size can be read in parallel and in pieces from disk or object storage. rs.scale.to_zarr_cube writes with spatial chunks and the whole time axis together (good for time series) and can append new dates, the usual pattern for monitoring.


Code
# Persist the cube as Zarr in two appends, then verify contents and size
store = OUT / "syracuse_s2_2025.zarr"
if store.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(store)
zcube = cube[["red", "green", "blue", "nir", "ndvi"]]
rs.scale.to_zarr_cube(zcube.isel(time=slice(0, 2)), store, chunks={"x": 512, "y": 512})          # July and August
rs.scale.to_zarr_cube(zcube.isel(time=slice(2, 3)), store, append_dim="time")                     # September arrives later
z = rs.scale.open_cube(store)
print("Dimensions:", dict(z.sizes), "| NDVI chunks:", z.ndvi.data.chunksize, "| CRS:", z.rio.crs)
print("Identical to the in-memory cube:", bool(np.allclose(z.ndvi.values, zcube.ndvi.values, equal_nan=True)))

# Compare Zarr store size to the original band GeoTIFFs
objects = [p for p in store.rglob("*") if p.is_file()]
zarr_mb = sum(p.stat().st_size for p in objects) / 1e6
tif_mb = sum((S2_DIR / sid / f"{b}.tif").stat().st_size for sid in SCENES for b in BANDS) / 1e6
print(f"Zarr store: {len(objects)} objects, {zarr_mb:.1f} MB (four bands + NDVI); "
      f"the 12 downloaded band GeoTIFFs: {tif_mb:.1f} MB")

from pyproj import Transformer
to_utm = Transformer.from_crs(4326, z.rio.crs, always_xy=True)

          "Residential south side": (-76.165, 43.031)}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
series = {name: z.ndvi.sel(x=to_utm.transform(*ll)[0], y=to_utm.transform(*ll)[1], method="nearest").load().to_series()
          for name, ll in points.items()}

The NDVI chunks are 2 × 512 × 512: the time chunk comes from the first write, which held two dates. Pixel time series were read lazily in a few hundredths of a second, because each touches only one spatial chunk.

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
text:
Publishing with STAC and GeoParquet
Products need a catalogue so others can find them. We write one NDVI COG per date and describe them with rs.scale.export_stac, which records each file’s footprint, date, projection and our own properties. The item footprints also go into a GeoParquet table, a compact index that can be filtered by bounding box without opening the catalogue (the idea behind stac-geoparquet).


Code
# Write per-date NDVI COGs and export a small STAC catalog for them
ndvi_files, dates = [], []
for t in cube.time.values:
    when = pd.Timestamp(t)
    path = OUT / f"ndvi_syracuse_{when:%Y%m%d}.tif"
    rs.write(cube.ndvi.sel(time=t).rio.write_crs(cube.rio.crs).rio.write_nodata(np.nan), path)
    ndvi_files.append(path); dates.append(when.tz_localize("UTC").to_pydatetime())
print("All NDVI products are valid COGs:", all(web.validate_cog(p).valid for p in ndvi_files))

# Build a STAC catalog pointing at the NDVI assets
catalog_dir = OUT / "stac"
if catalog_dir.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(catalog_dir)
cat_path = rs.scale.export_stac(ndvi_files, catalog_dir, collection_id="syracuse-ndvi-2025",
                                description="Cloud-masked Sentinel-2 NDVI, Syracuse NY, summer 2025",
                                datetimes=dates, properties={"platform": "sentinel-2", "product": "NDVI",
                                                             "source_collection": "sentinel-2-l2a"})
# Imports and configuration
import pystac
catalog = pystac.Catalog.from_file(str(cat_path))
items = list(next(catalog.get_children()).get_items())
pd.DataFrame([{"id": it.id, "datetime": it.datetime, "bbox": np.round(it.bbox, 3).tolist(),
               "proj": it.properties.get("proj:code") or it.properties.get("proj:epsg"),
               "asset": Path(it.assets["data"].get_absolute_href()).name} for it in items])

Each NDVI product is a valid COG. The STAC catalogue records every item’s footprint, date and projection (EPSG:32618), and links to its file. The GeoParquet index answers a footprint and date query (items over downtown in August) without opening the catalogue, then the matching COG is read: the mean August NDVI over a 2 × 2 km downtown box is 0.29, a mix of buildings, streets and street trees.
The same pattern scales to thousands of products: a STAC API or a stac-geoparquet table for discovery, and COGs or Zarr for the data.

title: Cloud-Native Rasters: COG, Zarr and STAC
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

get_images downloads clipped scenes with their STAC items; the item carries the scale, offset and no-data needed to use the pixels correctly.
A COG is tiled, has internal overviews, and keeps headers first and pixels ordered from coarse to fine; validate_cog checks each rule and to_cog produces it.
Lossless DEFLATE or ZSTD with a predictor is a good default; web-optimized COGs align with the XYZ tile grid.
Zarr stores n-dimensional cubes as chunked objects and supports appending new dates.
STAC describes products for discovery; a GeoParquet index of the footprints makes searches fast.

What we found

get_images downloaded three clipped Sentinel-2 scenes (72 MB). The clips are tiled but are not COGs; to_cog fixed that.
ZSTD or DEFLATE with a predictor made the smallest lossless COGs (14.9-15.9 MB from 16.1 MB of pixels plus two overview levels).
A remote re-read of the same window from AWS was pixel-identical to the download.
Earth Search has already removed Sentinel-2’s +1,000 offset (Planetary Computer has not), even though its item still lists it. Getting this wrong makes reflectance negative.
The Zarr cube appended a new date without rewriting, and a STAC catalogue with a GeoParquet index made the NDVI products searchable.

Exercises

Recompress the stack with blocksize=256 and compare file size and the number of tiles a 512 × 512 window touches.
Add compress="LERC" (lossy with a maximum error) or "WEBP" on an 8-bit RGB copy, and measure the size and the largest pixel error.
Use search_images to add the clearest 18TVN scene of October 2025, download it with get_images, and append it to the Zarr cube.
Write the NDVI cube to Zarr with chunks of {"time": 1, "x": 256, "y": 256} and time reading one full map versus one pixel’s time series. Which chunking suits which question?
Open the STAC catalogue in another tool (QGIS’s STAC browser or pystac-client) and check that the assets resolve.

References

Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF specification (OGC 21-026). https://docs.ogc.org/is/21-026/21-026.html
GDAL COG driver documentation. https://gdal.org/drivers/raster/cog.html
Zarr specification v2/v3. https://zarr.dev
STAC specification and best practices. https://stacspec.org
Cloud-Native Geospatial Foundation. Cloud-Optimized Geospatial Formats Guide. https://guide.cloudnativegeo.org

title: GeoLattice: Web & Cloud GIS
text:
An analysis that lives on one laptop helps one person. Web and cloud GIS takes it further: data are read straight from cloud storage without downloading whole files, processed next to the catalogue that holds them, and published as maps, tiles, APIs and small web applications that anyone with a browser can use. The same pipeline can then run on a schedule, tested and in a container.
These 12 notebooks are chapter 07 of the GeoLattice tutorials. They cover cloud-native rasters and vectors, spatial SQL, interactive web maps, map servers, geospatial APIs, web apps, scalable processing, cloud platforms and DevOps, and finish with a flood monitor for the haor basin of Bangladesh, using geolattice.web with the vector, raster and remote sensing modules.

title: GeoLattice: Web & Cloud GIS
text:
GeoLattice
GeoLattice is a Python library for geospatial analysis that brings vector and raster processing, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics, spatial databases, web and cloud GIS and remote sensing together under one import. It is built on GDAL, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely and xarray, so its functions take and return objects these libraries already use: GeoDataFrames, xarray DataArrays, NumPy arrays and GDAL-readable files.



Package
geolattice


Repository
github.com/zia207/GeoLattice


Python
3.10 or newer


License
MIT


Author
Zia Ahmed, Upatta Analytics



GDAL and PROJ must be installed first, with Python GDAL bindings that match the GDAL library (conda or your system package manager). Then install the web and remote sensing options:
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[web,rsense]"
The Earth Engine and openEO cells in the cloud platforms notebook need accounts with those services.

title: GeoLattice: Web & Cloud GIS
text:
Cloud-native data and serving
Cloud-native formats are laid out so that a client can fetch only the bytes it needs with HTTP range requests: a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) stores tiles and overviews in a fixed order, GeoParquet stores columns and row groups with bounding boxes, and PMTiles packs a whole tile pyramid into one file. geolattice.web writes and checks these formats, does the tile arithmetic and serves data as XYZ tiles and an OGC API.







Task
Functions (web)




Cloud access
to_vsi_path, cloud_env, cloud_options, remote_info


Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF
to_cog, validate_cog


Cloud-native vectors

Desktop, web and cloud GIS










Desktop GIS

Where data live
Local disk or a file server
A server database or file store

Where computing happens
The user’s computer
The server (rendering, queries)
Elastic clusters, GPUs and serverless functions, next to the data


How users reach it
Installed software (QGIS, ArcGIS Pro)
A browser or a mobile app
Notebooks, APIs and browsers


Scale
One user, one machine
Many users, modest data
Many users, petabytes


Typical Python tools
GeoPandas, rasterio, GeoLattice
Folium, leafmap, Streamlit, FastAPI
Dask, STAC, Zarr, Planetary Computer, Earth Engine



The shift from desktop to cloud is driven by data volume. The Landsat and Sentinel archives are several petabytes and grow by terabytes a day. Downloading them is impractical, so the modern pattern is the reverse: bring the code to the data, read only the pixels needed, and send results (maps, tables, tiles) to users.

title: Web/Cloud GIS
text:
Standards that connect the pieces
Standards let any client talk to any server. The Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) defines most of them; STAC and the tile conventions come from the community.








Standard
What it serves
Style




WMS (Web Map Service)
Rendered map images for a bounding box
Classic OGC, XML capabilities


WMTS (Web Map Tile Service)
Pre-cut map tiles
Classic OGC


WFS (Web Feature Service)
Vector features
Classic OGC, GML


WCS (Web Coverage Service)
Raster data values
Classic OGC


OGC API: Features / Tiles / Maps / Processes
The modern successors: features, tiles, maps, processing
REST + JSON, OpenAPI


XYZ / TMS tiles
256 × 256 images addressed by zoom, column and row
Community convention


TileJSON
Metadata for a tile layer (URL template, bounds, zooms)
Community (Mapbox)


STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog)
Catalogues of imagery and other assets
Community, JSON, now an OGC Community Standard


GeoJSON
Features in JSON
IETF RFC 7946



The rule of thumb today: OGC API + GeoJSON for vector services, XYZ tiles + TileJSON for maps, STAC for catalogues, COG / Zarr / GeoParquet for files.

title: Web/Cloud GIS
text:
Cloud-native reading: HTTP range requests
A web server normally sends a whole file. With an HTTP range request (Range: bytes=a-b) the client asks for only part of it, and the server answers 206 Partial Content. Cloud object stores all support this. A file is cloud-native when its layout lets a client find the bytes it needs from a small header: a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF stores its headers first and its pixels in independent tiles, so reading one area costs a few small requests.
First we ask the server about one Sentinel-2 band on AWS:


Code
# Inspect a public Sentinel-2 COG URL without downloading the whole file
COG_URL = ("https://sentinel-cogs.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/sentinel-s2-l2a-cogs/"
           "18/T/UN/2025/8/S2C_18TUN_20250802_0_L2A/B04.tif")
info = web.remote_info(COG_URL)

Now we read pixels with GDAL, which records how many bytes it downloads. We read twice: a 512 × 512 window over Syracuse at full resolution (10 m), and the whole 110 × 110 km tile from its smallest overview.


Code
# Compare bytes transferred for a local window vs a low-resolution overview
from osgeo import gdal
from pyproj import Transformer
gdal.UseExceptions()

def network_bytes():
    # Pull GDAL HTTP GET totals since the last NetworkStatsReset
    stats = json.loads(gdal.NetworkStatsGetAsSerializedJSON() or "{}")
    return stats.get("methods", {}).get("GET", {}).get("downloaded_bytes", 0), \
        stats.get("methods", {}).get("GET", {}).get("count", 0)

rows = []
with web.cloud_env(anonymous=True, CPL_VSIL_NETWORK_STATS_ENABLED="YES"):
    # Full-resolution 512x512 window centered near Syracuse
    gdal.NetworkStatsReset()
    ds = gdal.Open(web.to_vsi_path(COG_URL))
    band = ds.GetRasterBand(1)
    gt = ds.GetGeoTransform()
    x, y = Transformer.from_crs(4326, ds.GetSpatialRef().ExportToWkt(), always_xy=True).transform(-76.15, 43.05)
    col, row = int((x - gt[0]) / gt[1]) - 256, int((y - gt[3]) / gt[5]) - 256
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    window = band.ReadAsArray(col, row, 512, 512)
    got, calls = network_bytes()
    rows.append({"read": "512 × 512 window over Syracuse (10 m)", "pixels": window.size,
                 "bytes downloaded": got, "GET requests": calls, "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2)})

    # Whole tile from the coarsest overview (much fewer bytes)
    gdal.NetworkStatsReset()
    ovr = band.GetOverview(band.GetOverviewCount() - 1)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    overview = ovr.ReadAsArray()
    got, calls = network_bytes()
    rows.append({"read": f"whole tile from the smallest overview ({ovr.XSize} × {ovr.YSize})", "pixels": overview.size,
                 "bytes downloaded": got, "GET requests": calls, "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2)})
    full_size = ds.RasterXSize, ds.RasterYSize
    ds = None

reads = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("read")
reads["% of file"] = (reads["bytes downloaded"] / info["size"] * 100).round(2)
print(f"File: {info['size'] / 1e6:.1f} MB, {full_size[0]:,} × {full_size[1]:,} pixels")

The red band is a 91 MB file of 10,980 × 10,980 pixels, and the server answers range requests (status 206). Reading a 512 × 512 window over Syracuse transferred about 2.2 MB in two requests, 2.5% of the file. Reading the whole 110 × 110 km tile at its smallest overview transferred 0.29 MB, 0.3%.
The window cost more than its 0.5 MB of pixels because this COG is cut into 1,024 × 1,024 blocks: GDAL must fetch every block the window touches, here up to four. Block size is a design choice that Notebook 08_01 explores.
The overview image shows why overviews exist: a zoomed-out view of a whole Sentinel-2 tile needs only one small request. The black wedge on its left lies outside this orbit’s 290 km imaging swath. Timings (one to several seconds here) depend mostly on network latency, not on the number of bytes, which is why cloud-native reads try to need few requests.

title: Web/Cloud GIS
text:
The XYZ tile pyramid
Web maps cut the world into 256 × 256-pixel tiles in the Web Mercator projection. At zoom 0 one tile covers the world; each zoom level doubles the number of tiles in each direction. A tile is addressed by its zoom, column and row: {z}/{x}/{y}. geolattice.web implements the tile arithmetic.

    rows.append({"zoom": z, "tiles in the world": f"{4 ** z:,}",
                 "pixel size at equator (m)": round(web.tile_resolution(z), 2),
                 f"pixel size at {lat}°N (m)": round(web.tile_resolution(z, latitude=lat), 2),
                 "tile containing Syracuse": f"{t.z}/{t.x}/{t.y}",
                 "tiles covering Onondaga County": len(list(web.tiles_for_bounds(*onondaga.total_bounds, zooms=z)))})

Zoom whose pixels match each sensor at Syracuse:
  MODIS 250 m      → zoom 9
  Landsat 30 m     → zoom 12
  Sentinel-2 10 m  → zoom 14
  PlanetScope 3 m  → zoom 16
  NAIP 0.6 m       → zoom 18









Each zoom level halves the pixel size. At Syracuse’s latitude, map pixels match Landsat’s 30 m at zoom 12, Sentinel-2’s 10 m at zoom 14 and NAIP’s 0.6 m at zoom 18. Those are the deepest zooms worth rendering for each dataset; beyond them a tile server only enlarges pixels.
The number of tiles grows fourfold per level: Onondaga County fits in 9 tiles at zoom 10, 72 at zoom 12 and 896 at zoom 14. This growth is why tile servers render on demand and cache, rather than pre-rendering every level for large areas (Notebook 08_05).

title: Web/Cloud GIS
section: A web service in a few lines
text:
A web service in a few lines
A web GIS answers HTTP requests with JSON, images or HTML. geolattice.web.create_app builds a small server for vector layers (OGC API: Features) and rasters (XYZ tiles). We start one for the New York counties and talk to it the way a browser would, with Starlette’s test client (Notebook 08_05 runs it as a real server).


Code
# Spin up an in-process OGC API Features app and query counties near Syracuse
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

app = web.create_app(vectors={"ny_counties": counties}, title="New York counties")
client = TestClient(app)
landing = client.get("/").json()
print("Landing page links:", [l["rel"] for l in landing["links"]])
collection = client.get("/collections/ny_counties").json()
print("Collection extent:", [round(v, 3) for v in collection["extent"]["spatial"]["bbox"][0]])
r = client.get("/collections/ny_counties/items", params={"bbox": ",".join(map(str, SYRACUSE)), "limit": 10})
fc = r.json()
print(f"GET {r.url}\n→ {r.status_code} {r.headers['content-type']}: "
      f"{fc['numberMatched']} feature(s): {[f['properties']['COUNTY'] for f in fc['features']]}")

→ 200 application/geo+json: 1 feature(s): ['Onondaga County']


The same three requests work from any language or tool: a browser, curl, QGIS (which reads OGC API: Features directly), or JavaScript in a web page.

title: Web/Cloud GIS
text:
Cost, egress, licensing and location







Question
Why it matters




Egress
Cloud providers charge for data leaving their network (often around $0.05-0.09 per GB), not for reading inside the same region. Computing in the region where the data live (us-west-2 for Earth Search’s Sentinel-2) is cheaper and faster.


Requester pays
Some buckets (USGS Landsat on S3) bill the reader; cloud_env(requester_pays=True) acknowledges this.


Storage class and format
Cloud-native formats cut both transfer and compute; compressed COG and GeoParquet are often a third of the size of plain files.


Compute model
Always-on servers suit steady traffic; serverless functions suit bursts; clusters suit big batch jobs.


Licensing
Open data (Landsat, Copernicus) may be redistributed; commercial imagery usually may not be served publicly.


Data location (sovereignty)
Health, personal or government data may have to stay in a country or on premises; object storage like MinIO gives cloud-style access on local hardware.


Lock-in
Open formats (COG, Zarr, GeoParquet) and open standards (STAC, OGC API) keep data and code portable between providers.

Capstone



Key ideas

Cloud GIS brings computing to the data; web GIS brings results to users.
Open standards (OGC API, STAC, XYZ tiles, GeoJSON) let any client use any server.
Cloud-native formats plus HTTP range requests let a program read a small part of a large remote file.
Every web map is a pyramid of 256 × 256 tiles addressed by {z}/{x}/{y}.
Catalogues tell you what exists before you download anything; get_images searches five of them.

What we measured

Reading a 512 × 512 window from a 91 MB remote Sentinel-2 band transferred about 2.2 MB (2.5%); an overview of the whole tile transferred 0.29 MB.
Onondaga County needs 9 tiles at zoom 10 and 896 at zoom 14; Sentinel-2’s 10 m pixels match zoom 14 at this latitude.
One search found 302 Sentinel-2 and 38 Landsat scenes for the 2025 season, and the latest NAIP (2022), without downloading any imagery.

title: Cloud-Native Vectors: GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf and PMTiles
text:
Why not shapefiles and GeoJSON?
The shapefile (1990s, Esri) is still the most common GIS file, but it is a bundle of separate files, has a 2 GB limit per file, stores attributes in an old dBASE table with 10-character field names, has no compression, and keeps no spatial index unless extra index files are made. GeoJSON is a single text file that every web tool reads, but it is large (coordinates are written as text) and has to be parsed from start to end.


Code
# Show shapefile sidecar sizes and the classic 10-character field-name limit
parts = sorted(BD.glob("bd_union_GCS.*"))
print(f"One shapefile = {len(parts)} files, {sum(p.stat().st_size for p in parts) / 1e6:.1f} MB:")
for p in parts:
    print(f"  {p.name:22s} {p.stat().st_size / 1e6:8.2f} MB")
long_names = [c for c in unions.columns if len(c) == 10]
print("Field names cut to 10 characters:", long_names)

Field names such as ADM4ALT1EN and ADM4ALT2EN are abbreviations forced by the 10-character limit (alternative English names 1 and 2). The modern formats below keep full names, typed columns and one file per dataset.

Writing cloud-native formats
We write the same 5,160 unions in seven ways and compare file size, write time and the time to read the whole file back.

# Export unions to several formats and benchmark write/read size and speed
writers = {
    "GeoJSON":                  ("unions.geojson",          lambda p: unions.to_file(p, driver="GeoJSON")),
    "GeoJSON Sequence":         ("unions.geojsonl",         lambda p: unions.to_file(p, driver="GeoJSONSeq")),
    "GeoPackage":               ("unions.gpkg",             lambda p: unions.to_file(p, driver="GPKG", layer="unions")),
    "FlatGeobuf":               ("unions.fgb",              lambda p: write_flatgeobuf(p, unions)),
    "GeoParquet (WKB, zstd)":   ("unions.parquet",          lambda p: write_geoparquet(p, unions, row_group_size=256)),
    "GeoParquet (WKB, snappy)": ("unions_snappy.parquet",   lambda p: write_geoparquet(p, unions, compression="snappy", row_group_size=256)),
    "GeoParquet (GeoArrow, zstd)": ("unions_geoarrow.parquet", lambda p: write_geoparquet(p, unions, geometry_encoding="geoarrow", row_group_size=256)),
}

           ".parquet": read_geoparquet}

The same 5,160 unions take very different space:

GeoJSON is 343 MB, 2.7 times the shapefile, because every coordinate is written as text. It took about 12 s to write and 6 s to read.
GeoJSON Sequence is smaller (219 MB, without indentation) but just as slow to parse.
GeoPackage and FlatGeobuf are about the shapefile’s size (130 and 126 MB) and read in under 0.2 s.
GeoParquet is the smallest: 103 MB with zstd compression, 108 MB with snappy, and 98 MB with the GeoArrow geometry encoding, which stores coordinates as plain numeric arrays rather than WKB blobs. It reads as fast as the binary formats.

Polygon coordinates are dense floating-point numbers that compress only modestly. For tables with many attribute columns, GeoParquet’s advantage is much larger.

title: Cloud-Native Vectors: GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf and PMTiles
text:
Inside a GeoParquet file
A GeoParquet file is a Parquet table with a geo metadata entry. Rows are grouped into row groups; inside each group every column is stored and compressed separately, and the footer records each column’s minimum and maximum per group. GeoParquet 1.1 adds a bbox covering column (bbox.xmin, bbox.ymin, bbox.xmax, bbox.ymax for every feature), so the footer statistics describe the extent of each row group. write_geoparquet also sorts features along a Hilbert curve, so that nearby features end up in the same row group.


Code
# Inspect GeoParquet metadata: encoding, row groups, CRS, and columns
info = web.geoparquet_info(OUT / "unions.parquet")
display(pd.Series({k: info[k] for k in ["version", "primary_column", "encoding", "geometry_types", "covering",
                                        "num_rows", "num_row_groups"]}, name="unions.parquet").to_frame())
print("CRS:", info["crs"].name, "| columns:", ", ".join(info["columns"][:8]), "…")
