One heavy request takes about 0.5 s. With eight running at once:

def endpoint: the eight heavy requests ran in the thread pool and finished within 0.58 s (k-d tree queries and NumPy release the GIL for much of the work). /health kept answering, 26 times, in at most 18 ms.
async def endpoint: the same code ran on the event loop, one request after another. The slowest heavy request took 3.94 s, eight times the work of one, and /health got a single answer, after 3.9 s. For that whole time the server could not answer anyone.

For CPU work, write def, or hand the work to a background job or a worker pool.

title: Building Geospatial APIs with FastAPI
text:
Testing the API
An API is a contract; automated tests check that it keeps it. FastAPI’s TestClient makes tests ordinary Python functions, run by pytest in a project (tests/test_api.py). Here they run directly. Each test checks one promise of the API.


Code
# Automated checks of key endpoints (locate, districts, soil, NDVI, zonal auth, OpenAPI)
tc = TestClient(app)
tc.__enter__()

def test_health():
    assert tc.get("/health").json()["status"] == "ok"

def test_locate_known_point():
    r = tc.get("/locate", params={"lon": 90.41, "lat": 23.78})
    assert r.status_code == 200 and r.json()["district"] == "Dhaka" and r.json()["division"] == "Dhaka"

def test_locate_rejects_points_outside_the_box():
    assert tc.get("/locate", params={"lon": 100, "lat": 23}).status_code == 422

def test_locate_sea_is_not_found():
    assert tc.get("/locate", params={"lon": 90.5, "lat": 21.0}).status_code == 404

def test_district_lookup_is_case_insensitive_and_suggests():
    assert tc.get("/districts/RANGPUR").status_code == 200
    r = tc.get("/districts/Rangpor")
    assert r.status_code == 404 and "Rangpur" in r.json()["detail"]["suggestions"]

def test_districts_filters_and_sorting():
    rows = tc.get("/districts", params={"division": "Sylhet", "sort": "poverty_pct"}).json()
    assert len(rows) == 4 and [r["poverty_pct"] for r in rows] == sorted(r["poverty_pct"] for r in rows)

def test_soil_estimate_is_within_sample_range():
    s = tc.get("/soil/estimate", params={"lon": 89.37, "lat": 24.85}).json()
    assert store.soil[:, 0].min() <= s["ph"] <= store.soil[:, 0].max() and s["neighbours"] == 12

def test_timeseries_respects_dates():
    ts = tc.get("/ndvi/timeseries", params={"lon": 89.37, "lat": 24.85, "start": "2020-01-01", "end": "2020-12-31"}).json()
    assert ts["n"] == 23 and all(d.startswith("2020") for d in ts["dates"])

def test_zonal_requires_key_and_valid_geometry():
    assert tc.post("/ndvi/zonal", json={"geometry": square}).status_code == 401
    time.sleep(0.6)
    bad = {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[90.3, 23.7], [90.5, 23.7], [90.5, 23.9]]]}
    assert tc.post("/ndvi/zonal", json={"geometry": bad}, headers=headers).status_code == 422

def test_zonal_matches_direct_computation():
    time.sleep(0.6)
    r = tc.post("/ndvi/zonal", json={"geometry": square, "date": "2020-08-15"}, headers=headers).json()
    t = int(np.abs(store.dates - pd.Timestamp("2020-08-15")).argmin())
    v = store.ndvi[t][polygon_pixels(shape(square))]
    assert r["pixels"] == int((v != 0).sum()) and abs(r["mean"] - v[v != 0].mean() / 1e4) < 1e-3

def test_openapi_lists_every_endpoint():
    paths = tc.get("/openapi.json").json()["paths"]
    assert {"/locate", "/soil/estimate", "/ndvi/zonal", "/jobs/ndvi-trend", "/jobs/{job_id}"} <= set(paths)

title: Building Geospatial APIs with FastAPI
text:
From notebook to deployment
In a project, the API is a package rather than notebook cells:
bd_api/
├── app/
│   ├── main.py          # FastAPI(), middleware, routers included, lifespan
│   ├── data.py          # GeoStore: loading and indexes
│   ├── security.py      # require_key, RateLimiter
│   └── routers/         # districts.py, spatial.py, ndvi.py, jobs.py (APIRouter each)
├── tests/test_api.py    # the tests of Section 11
├── pyproject.toml
└── Dockerfile           # Notebook 08_10
It runs with uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4 (several processes, as measured in Notebook 08_05), behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer) that terminates HTTPS.








Concern
In this notebook
In production




Secrets
A key generated in memory
Environment variables or a secret manager; keys per client, revocable


Rate limits
In-memory token bucket
Shared store (Redis) across workers, or the API gateway


Jobs
Background tasks in the server process, results in a dict
A task queue (Celery, RQ, Arq) with workers, results in object storage, job records in a database


Data
In memory per process
A database (PostGIS), COGs and Zarr in object storage


Observability
/health
Structured logs, metrics (latency percentiles, error rates), tracing


Documentation
/docs
The same, plus examples and a versioned URL (/v1/...)

title: Building Geospatial APIs with FastAPI
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

FastAPI turns typed Python functions into documented, validated HTTP endpoints; Pydantic and geojson_pydantic reject bad input with clear 422 errors before any analysis runs.
Load data once (lifespan) and index it: R-trees for polygons, k-d trees for points, arrays for rasters.
Use the right status codes: 404 for “no such thing”, 422 for invalid input, 401 and 429 for access control, 202 plus a job URL for long work.
async def is for waiting, not computing: CPU work belongs in def endpoints, background jobs or separate worker processes.
Mount standard services (OGC API) and web pages next to custom endpoints; test the API as a contract.

What we built and measured

Eleven endpoints over 64 districts, 5,160 unions, 263 arsenic fields, 37,923 soil samples and 572 MODIS NDVI images, loaded in about 5 s at start-up.
Soil estimates by IDW: pH MAE 0.43 in leave-one-out validation, against 0.91 without location.
Zonal statistics and NDVI trend jobs; Dhaka showed significant greenness decline in 22.9% of its pixels from 2001 to 2024, Bogra significant increases in 84.1%.
API keys (401), a token-bucket rate limit (429), gzip (2.9-8.2× smaller) and CORS.
An async def endpoint doing CPU work stalled the whole server for 3.9 s; the same code in a def endpoint kept /health under 18 ms.
Eleven automated tests, all passing.

Exercises

Add /upazilas/{name} with poverty from Notebook 08_03’s poverty_clean, returning 409 when a name is ambiguous (several upazilas share it) and listing the candidates.
Add a format query parameter to /ndvi/timeseries that returns CSV (text/csv) as well as JSON.
Return a confidence interval with /soil/estimate, from the leave-one-out errors of Section 6 at similar distances to the nearest sample.
Make /ndvi/zonal accept several dates at once and return a table; limit the number of dates.
Replace the in-memory job store with files (one JSON per job) so jobs survive a restart, and run the API with --workers 2. What goes wrong with the in-memory version?

References

FastAPI documentation. https://fastapi.tiangolo.com
Pydantic documentation. https://docs.pydantic.dev
geojson-pydantic. https://github.com/developmentseed/geojson-pydantic
Fielding, R. T. (2000). Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures (REST), ch. 5. University of California, Irvine.
Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall’s tau. JASA, 63, 1379-1389.
Didan, K. (2021). MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 250m SIN Grid V061 (MOD13Q1). NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC.

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
text:
Scaling in one page








Bottleneck
Symptom
Remedy




Computation (CPU-bound)
One core at 100 %
Parallel processes (Dask, multiprocessing), vectorisation, GPUs


Memory bandwidth
More cores stop helping well before all are busy
Smaller chunks that fit in cache, fewer temporary arrays, GPUs (much higher bandwidth)


Memory capacity
Out-of-memory errors
Chunked, lazy processing (Dask), out-of-core formats (Zarr)


Disk or network input/output
Cores idle while waiting
Concurrent requests, cloud-optimised formats, compute next to the data


Python’s GIL
Threads do not run Python code in parallel
Processes, or libraries that release the GIL (NumPy, GDAL)



Amdahl’s law: if a fraction p of the work can run in parallel, N workers give at most a speed-up of 1 / ((1 − p) + p / N). With p = 0.95, even infinite workers give 20×. Scaling therefore starts with measuring which part of the job takes the time.
Tools. On one machine: concurrent.futures, joblib, Dask (LocalCluster), CuPy and RAPIDS for GPUs. On clusters: Dask (Kubernetes, HPC, Coiled, Dask Gateway), Ray, Spark with Apache Sedona. As managed services: AWS Batch, Google Cloud Run jobs and Batch, Azure Batch, serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions), and platforms such as Planetary Computer, Earth Engine or openEO (Notebook 08_09).

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
section: The workload and its input: reading 572 images
text:
The workload and its input: reading 572 images
Every run starts by reading the images. The 572 GeoTIFFs (LZW-compressed, 670 × 480 pixels) are read serially, with 16 threads, and with 8 processes.


Code
# Time a naive loop that opens all 572 MODIS NDVI GeoTIFFs
def read_one(path):
    with rasterio.open(path) as src:
        return src.read(1)

timings = {}
t0 = time.perf_counter(); cube = np.stack([read_one(f) for f in files]); timings["serial"] = time.perf_counter() - t0
with ThreadPoolExecutor(16) as ex:
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); c2 = np.stack(list(ex.map(read_one, files))); timings["16 threads"] = time.perf_counter() - t0
with ProcessPoolExecutor(8) as ex:
    list(ex.map(read_one, files[:8]))                                     # start the workers first
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); c3 = np.stack(list(ex.map(read_one, files, chunksize=8))); timings["8 processes"] = time.perf_counter() - t0
assert (c2 == cube).all() and (c3 == cube).all()
with rasterio.open(files[0]) as src:
    crs, transform, shape = src.crs, src.transform, src.shape
print(f"cube {cube.shape}, {cube.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB in memory")
pd.Series(timings, name="seconds").round(2).to_frame()


cube (572, 670, 480), 368 MB in memory









seconds




serial
3.28


16 threads
4.36


8 processes
0.66







Threads made reading slower (4.4 s against 3.3 s serially), while 8 processes made it five times faster (0.66 s). Decompressing the files releases Python’s GIL, but rasterio holds it while opening each file, so threads mostly queue for it. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and lock. Which kind of parallelism helps depends on the library, so measure it.

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
section: Lazy pipelines with xarray and Dask
text:
Lazy pipelines with xarray and Dask
The trend is computed on monthly anomalies: monthly mean NDVI minus that month’s long-term mean, which removes the seasonal cycle. With xarray and Dask the whole pipeline is written first and only evaluated at the end, chunk by chunk. Nothing is read until .compute() is called.


Code
# Lazy xarray/Dask monthly anomaly pipeline vs eager NumPy on the in-memory cube
t0 = time.perf_counter()
lazy = xr.concat([rioxarray.open_rasterio(f, chunks={"x": 240, "y": 335}).squeeze("band", drop=True) for f in files],
                 dim=pd.Index(dates, name="time"))
ndvi = (lazy.where(lazy != 0) / 1e4).astype("float32")              # 0 marks pixels outside Bangladesh
monthly = ndvi.resample(time="MS").mean()
anomaly = monthly.groupby("time.month") - monthly.groupby("time.month").mean()
build_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
graph = anomaly.data.__dask_graph__()
print(f"pipeline defined in {build_s:.1f} s: {len(graph):,} tasks, {anomaly.data.npartitions} output chunks, "
      f"shape {anomaly.shape}, nothing computed yet")

# Compute the Dask graph with 8 threads
with dask.config.set(scheduler="threads", num_workers=8):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); anom_dask = anomaly.compute(); dask_s = time.perf_counter() - t0

# Same monthly anomalies with eager NumPy for a correctness check
t0 = time.perf_counter()                                              # the same in eager NumPy, from the cube in memory
v = cube.astype("float32") / 1e4
v[cube == 0] = np.nan
months = dates.to_period("M")
codes, uniq = pd.factorize(months)
mon = np.stack([np.nanmean(v[codes == k], axis=0) for k in range(len(uniq))])
moy = np.array([p.month for p in uniq])
clim = np.stack([np.nanmean(mon[moy == m], axis=0) for m in range(1, 13)])
anom_np = mon - clim[moy - 1]
numpy_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"Dask (read + compute, 8 threads): {dask_s:.1f} s | NumPy on the cube already in memory: {numpy_s:.1f} s")
print("largest difference between the two:", float(np.nanmax(np.abs(anom_dask.values - anom_np))))


pipeline defined in 5.7 s: 31,165 tasks, 1196 output chunks, shape (299, 670, 480), nothing computed yet
Dask (read + compute, 8 threads): 13.4 s | NumPy on the cube already in memory: 1.6 s
largest difference between the two: 2.980232238769531e-07


The lazy pipeline is a graph of 31,165 tasks over 1,196 chunks, defined in 5.7 s without reading any pixel data (the time goes into opening the 572 file headers). Computing it with 8 threads took 13.4 s and matched NumPy to 3 × 10⁻⁷. NumPy on the cube already in memory took 1.6 s, so for data that fit in memory, eager NumPy wins. Dask’s value is elsewhere: the same code runs when the cube is 100 times larger than memory, or on a cluster. Its threaded reads also meet the rasterio GIL problem of Section 3, which a process-based scheduler avoids.
The trend needs only land pixels. We keep pixels that have NDVI on at least 90 % of dates and arrange the anomalies as a matrix of months × pixels: the input of everything that follows.


Code

land = (cube != 0).mean(axis=0) >= 0.9
A = np.ascontiguousarray(anom_np[:, land]).astype("float32")          # (months, pixels)
n_months, n_pix = A.shape
pairs = n_months * (n_months - 1) // 2
np.save(OUT / "anomalies.npy", A)
print(f"{n_pix:,} land pixels x {n_months} months; {pairs:,} pairs per pixel; "
      f"{pairs * n_pix / 1e9:.1f} billion slopes in total; matrix {A.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB")

section: Chunks matter: the same cube in two Zarr layouts
text:
Chunks matter: the same cube in two Zarr layouts
Zarr stores an array as a grid of compressed chunks, each a separate object, which is how large arrays live in cloud storage. A reader fetches whole chunks, so the chunk shape decides which questions are cheap. We store the NDVI cube twice: chunked by date (one map per chunk, as images arrive) and chunked by space (all dates of a small tile per chunk, for time series), and time the two typical reads.


Code
# Zarr chunk layout trade-off: fast time series vs fast spatial slices
layouts = {"by date (1 x 670 x 480)": (1, 670, 480), "by space (572 x 64 x 64)": (572, 64, 64)}
rows = []
row, col = 198, 137                                           # a pixel near Bogra
for name, chunks in layouts.items():
    path = OUT / f"ndvi_{chunks[0]}x{chunks[1]}.zarr"
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    z = zarr.create_array(store=str(path), shape=cube.shape, chunks=chunks, dtype="int16")
    z[:] = cube
    write_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
    z = zarr.open_array(str(path), mode="r")
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); series = z[:, row, col]; series_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); one_map = z[300]; map_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    n_files = sum(1 for p in path.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
    rows.append({"layout": name, "chunks (files)": n_files, "MB on disk": round(sum(p.stat().st_size for p in path.rglob('*') if p.is_file()) / 1e6, 1),
                 "write s": round(write_s, 1), "one pixel, all dates (ms)": round(series_ms, 1), "one date, all pixels (ms)": round(map_ms, 1)})
    assert (series == cube[:, row, col]).all() and (one_map == cube[300]).all()

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
text:
Parallel computation with Dask
The kernel computes, for a block of pixels, the slopes between all pairs of months and takes their median. It is plain NumPy, so it runs unchanged on one core, in many processes, or (Section 7) on a GPU.


Code
# Theil-Sen per pixel (NDVI per decade); time a 20k-pixel serial baseline
def theil_sen(a, xp=np):
    "Median of all pairwise slopes for each column of a (months x pixels); NDVI per decade."
    n = a.shape[0]
    i, j = xp.triu_indices(n, 1)
    slopes = (a[j] - a[i]) / (j - i).astype("float32")[:, None]
    return (xp.nanmedian(slopes, axis=0) * 120).astype("float32")

SUB = 20_000                                                    # a subset for the scaling experiments
t0 = time.perf_counter()
ref = np.concatenate([theil_sen(A[:, k:k + 250]) for k in range(0, SUB, 250)])
serial_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"serial: {serial_s:.1f} s for {SUB:,} pixels = {serial_s / SUB * 1000:.2f} ms per pixel; "
      f"all {n_pix:,} pixels would take about {serial_s / SUB * n_pix:.0f} s")


serial: 13.6 s for 20,000 pixels = 0.68 ms per pixel; all 145,672 pixels would take about 99 s


Dask splits the pixels into chunks and runs one task per chunk on a cluster of worker processes (LocalCluster here; the same code runs on a cloud cluster by pointing Client at it). The input is read by each worker from a memory-mapped file instead of being copied into the task graph. We vary the number of workers and the chunk size on the 20,000-pixel subset.


Code
# Scale Theil-Sen with Dask LocalCluster; plot speed-up vs ideal and Amdahl curves
np.save(OUT / "subset.npy", A[:, :SUB])
rows = []
for workers in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]:
    with LocalCluster(n_workers=workers, threads_per_worker=1, processes=True, dashboard_address=None,
                      silence_logs=logging.CRITICAL) as cluster, Client(cluster):
        for chunk in ([250, 1000] if workers in (8, 16) else [250]):
            x = da.from_array(np.load(OUT / "subset.npy", mmap_mode="r"), chunks=(n_months, chunk), asarray=True)
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            res = x.map_blocks(theil_sen, drop_axis=0, dtype="float32").compute()
            sec = time.perf_counter() - t0
            assert np.allclose(res, ref, equal_nan=True)
            rows.append({"workers": workers, "chunk (pixels)": chunk, "tasks": SUB // chunk, "seconds": sec,
                         "speed-up": serial_s / sec, "efficiency": serial_s / sec / workers})
scaling = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(scaling.round(2))

# Speed-up plot for 250-pixel chunks
best = scaling[scaling["chunk (pixels)"] == 250]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.plot(best.workers, best["speed-up"], "o-", label="measured (chunks of 250 pixels)")
ax.plot(best.workers, best.workers, "--", color="grey", label="ideal")
for p in [0.95, 0.85]:
    ax.plot(best.workers, 1 / ((1 - p) + p / best.workers), ":", label=f"Amdahl, p = {p}")
ax.set_xlabel("worker processes"); ax.set_ylabel("speed-up over one core"); ax.set_xticks(best.workers)
ax.set_title("Theil-Sen trend on 20,000 pixels"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)

The laptop’s 16 physical cores also share caches and memory channels. Measured scaling, not the core count, tells you how many workers are worth paying for.

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
section: The same kernel on a GPU
text:
The same kernel on a GPU
CuPy mirrors NumPy’s interface on NVIDIA GPUs, so theil_sen(a, xp=cp) runs the same code there. Each block of pixels is copied to the GPU, processed, and the result copied back. We time the copy and the computation separately, then process all land pixels on the GPU and with Dask on the CPU.


Code
# Full-country Theil-Sen: optional GPU, then Dask with 8 workers; compare wall times
# Optional CuPy path: measure copy + compute cost, then full-array timing
if GPU:
    theil_sen(cp.asarray(A[:, :100]), xp=cp); cp.cuda.Device().synchronize()      # compile kernels once
    rows = []
    for block in [1000, 2000, 4000]:
        blk = A[:, :block]
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); g = cp.asarray(blk); cp.cuda.Device().synchronize(); up = time.perf_counter() - t0
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); r = theil_sen(g, xp=cp); cp.cuda.Device().synchronize(); comp = time.perf_counter() - t0
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); r = r.get(); down = time.perf_counter() - t0
        rows.append({"block (pixels)": block, "copy to GPU ms": up * 1000, "compute ms": comp * 1000, "copy back ms": down * 1000,
                     "ms per 1,000 pixels": (up + comp + down) / block * 1e6,
                     "GPU memory used GB": round((block * pairs * 4 * 2) / 1e9, 2)})
        assert np.allclose(r, ref[:block], equal_nan=True, atol=1e-5)
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1))

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    trend_gpu = np.concatenate([theil_sen(cp.asarray(A[:, k:k + 2000]), xp=cp).get() for k in range(0, n_pix, 2000)])
    gpu_full = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"GPU, all {n_pix:,} pixels: {gpu_full:.1f} s")
else:
    trend_gpu, gpu_full = None, None
    print("No CUDA GPU: skipped")

# Dask LocalCluster over all land pixels
with LocalCluster(n_workers=8, threads_per_worker=1, processes=True, dashboard_address=None,
                      silence_logs=logging.CRITICAL) as cluster, Client(cluster):
    x = da.from_array(np.load(OUT / "anomalies.npy", mmap_mode="r"), chunks=(n_months, 250), asarray=True)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    trend = x.map_blocks(theil_sen, drop_axis=0, dtype="float32").compute()
    dask_full = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"Dask, 8 workers, all {n_pix:,} pixels: {dask_full:.1f} s")

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
section: Reading from the cloud in parallel
text:
Reading from the cloud in parallel
In the cloud the input is usually remote. A STAC search finds every Sentinel-2 scene of tile 18TVN (Syracuse, NY) with less than 20 % cloud between April and October 2025; we then read the same 12 km window of the red band from 12 of them, serially and with 4, 8 and 16 threads, counting the bytes GDAL downloads. GDAL’s Python bindings release the GIL during reads, so threads can overlap the waiting.


Code
# Remote COG window reads via STAC + GDAL /vsicurl; scale with thread pools
# STAC search + GDAL config for range reads of remote COGs
from pystac_client import Client as STACClient
import pyproj

BOX = (-76.20, 43.00, -76.08, 43.08)
OPTIONS = dict(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN="EMPTY_DIR", AWS_NO_SIGN_REQUEST="YES", GDAL_HTTP_MULTIRANGE="YES",
               GDAL_HTTP_MERGE_CONSECUTIVE_RANGES="YES", CPL_VSIL_CURL_ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS=".tif",
               CPL_VSIL_NETWORK_STATS_ENABLED="YES", VSI_CACHE="FALSE", CPL_VSIL_CURL_NON_CACHED="/vsicurl/")
for k, v in OPTIONS.items():
    gdal.SetConfigOption(k, v)

# Read one bbox window and return its mean
def read_window(href):
    "Read the BOX window of a remote COG band with GDAL; return its mean."
    ds = gdal.Open("/vsicurl/" + href)
    gt = ds.GetGeoTransform()
    tr = pyproj.Transformer.from_crs(4326, ds.GetSpatialRef().ExportToWkt(), always_xy=True)
    (x0, y1), (x1, y0) = tr.transform(BOX[0], BOX[3]), tr.transform(BOX[2], BOX[1])
    c0, r0 = int((x0 - gt[0]) / gt[1]), int((y1 - gt[3]) / gt[5])
    c1, r1 = int((x1 - gt[0]) / gt[1]), int((y0 - gt[3]) / gt[5])
    return float(ds.GetRasterBand(1).ReadAsArray(c0, r0, c1 - c0, r1 - r0).mean())

def downloaded():
    stats = json.loads(gdal.NetworkStatsGetAsSerializedJSON() or "{}")
    return sum(m.get("downloaded_bytes", 0) for m in stats.get("methods", {}).values())

# Search Sentinel-2, then time threaded window reads
try:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    items = list(STACClient.open("https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1").search(
        collections=["sentinel-2-l2a"], bbox=BOX, datetime="2025-04-01/2025-10-31", query={"eo:cloud_cover": {"lt": 20}}).items())
    tile = [it for it in items if it.properties.get("mgrs:utm_zone") == 18 and it.properties.get("mgrs:grid_square") == "VN"]
    hrefs = [it.assets["red"].href for it in sorted(tile, key=lambda it: it.datetime)][:12]
    print(f"STAC search: {len(items)} scenes, {len(tile)} on tile 18TVN, in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; reading {len(hrefs)}")
    rows = []
    for threads in [1, 4, 8, 16]:
        gdal.NetworkStatsReset()
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        if threads == 1:
            means = [read_window(h) for h in hrefs]
        else:
            with ThreadPoolExecutor(threads) as ex:
                means = list(ex.map(read_window, hrefs))
        sec = time.perf_counter() - t0
        mb = downloaded() / 1e6
        rows.append({"threads": threads, "seconds": sec, "MB downloaded": mb, "MB/s": mb / sec})
    remote = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("threads")
    remote["speed-up"] = remote.seconds.iloc[0] / remote.seconds
    display(remote.round(2))
except Exception as exc:
    remote = None
    print("Remote reads skipped:", type(exc).__name__, exc)

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
section: Batch jobs: the serverless pattern, and what a run costs
text:
Batch jobs: the serverless pattern, and what a run costs
Cloud batch services (AWS Batch, Google Cloud Batch and Cloud Run jobs, Azure Batch) and serverless functions all run the same unit: an independent job that reads its piece of input from object storage, writes its own output, and exits. A coordinator starts one job per piece (a job array) and combines the outputs. Jobs must be idempotent: re-running one gives the same output, so failed or duplicated jobs are harmless.
We imitate this with separate operating-system processes: the trend calculation is split into 8 jobs by pixel range, each a fresh Python process with its own arguments, as a container would be.


Code
# Idempotent batch jobs: split pixels across processes, re-run, and recover a "lost" part
job_code = '''import json, sys, time
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

def theil_sen(a):
    n = a.shape[0]
    i, j = np.triu_indices(n, 1)
    return (np.nanmedian((a[j] - a[i]) / (j - i).astype("float32")[:, None], axis=0) * 120).astype("float32")

src, start, stop, out = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3]), Path(sys.argv[4])
done = out.with_suffix(".json")
if done.exists():                                   # idempotent: finished jobs are skipped
    sys.exit(0)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
a = np.load(src, mmap_mode="r")
res = np.concatenate([theil_sen(np.asarray(a[:, k:min(k + 250, stop)])) for k in range(start, stop, 250)])
np.save(out, res)
done.write_text(json.dumps({"start": start, "stop": stop, "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}))
'''
(OUT / "trend_job.py").write_text(job_code)
jobs_dir = OUT / "jobs"; jobs_dir.mkdir()
bounds = np.linspace(0, n_pix, 9).astype(int)

# Launch one process per pixel slice
def run_jobs():
    procs = [subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, str(OUT / "trend_job.py"), str(OUT / "anomalies.npy"), str(a), str(b),
                               str(jobs_dir / f"part_{k:02d}.npy")]) for k, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(bounds[:-1], bounds[1:]))]
    return [p.wait() for p in procs]

t0 = time.perf_counter(); codes = run_jobs(); wall = time.perf_counter() - t0
manifest = [json.loads(p.read_text()) for p in sorted(jobs_dir.glob("*.json"))]

print("identical to the Dask result:", np.allclose(combined, trend, equal_nan=True))
t0 = time.perf_counter(); run_jobs(); print(f"re-run: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s (all jobs already done, nothing recomputed)")
(jobs_dir / "part_03.json").unlink()                 # pretend job 3 failed
t0 = time.perf_counter(); run_jobs(); print(f"after 'losing' job 3: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s (only job 3 ran again)")
job_cpu_s = sum(m["seconds"] for m in manifest)

The 8 independent jobs finished in 17.1 s, slightly faster than Dask (20.1 s) because they skip the scheduler. Each job took about 16-17 s against roughly 12 s if it had the machine to itself: the memory-bandwidth contention of Section 6 again. Re-running did nothing (0.1 s), because every job found its completion record. After one record was deleted, only that job ran again (13.3 s). This is what makes retries and spot or preemptible instances safe.
With the illustrative prices, the whole national trend costs a fraction of a cent per run, from USD 0.0012 (one vCPU, sequential) to 0.0044 (eight serverless functions). For a job this size the price hardly matters: time and simplicity decide. The ranking matters at scale:

Parallel CPU runs cost more than sequential ones, because imperfect scaling wastes resource-seconds: 161 against 99 vCPU-seconds.
Serverless charges a premium for its convenience.
A GPU is fastest, and cheaper per run than parallel CPU only when it is kept busy.

Before scaling out to many machines, remember what the measurements showed. Most of the gain came from using this machine well (processes, the right chunk size, a GPU), and the network, not the number of cores, limited remote reads. Scale out when one machine’s memory, disk or bandwidth is exhausted, and move the computation to the data’s region rather than the data to the computation.

title: Scalable Processing: Dask, GPUs and Batch Jobs
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Measure first: the slow part may be reading, memory bandwidth or the network rather than arithmetic.
Dask builds lazy, chunked pipelines that run on threads, processes or clusters with the same code.
Chunk shape decides which reads are cheap: chunk for the access pattern you serve.
Processes avoid the GIL; speed-up then stops at a limit set by the hardware (Amdahl’s law in practice).
GPUs suit regular, data-parallel kernels; CuPy runs NumPy-style code on them with few changes.
Batch jobs that are independent and idempotent are the unit of serverless and cloud batch processing; cost follows resource-time.

What we measured on one laptop-class machine (16 cores, one GPU)

Reading 572 images: 3.3 s serially, 4.4 s with threads (GIL), 0.66 s with 8 processes.
Zarr chunks: a pixel’s time series took 182 ms chunked by date against 5.5 ms chunked by space; a single map the reverse (1.1 against 41 ms).
Theil-Sen on 145,672 pixels: 99 s on one core, 20.1 s with Dask (4.9×), 9.9 s on the GPU (10×). Dask scaling flattened beyond 4-8 workers (memory bandwidth).
Result: 69.5% of land pixels greened by more than 0.02 NDVI per decade; browning followed rivers and cities.
Remote reads: the network saturated at about 5 MB/s, so 8 threads gave 2.5× and 16 no more.
Batch jobs: 8 independent, idempotent jobs took 17.1 s and re-ran only what was missing; a full run costs well under one US cent at illustrative prices.

Exercises

Replace nanmedian by np.partition-based medians (no NaNs after filtering). How much faster is the CPU kernel, and does the Dask speed-up curve change?
Compute the Mann-Kendall statistic alongside the Theil-Sen slope on the GPU, and map pixels with significant trends (take care: monthly anomalies are autocorrelated).
Rechunk the Zarr store to (572, 128, 128) with dask.array.rechunk and repeat the read timings of Section 5. What is the trade-off?
Run Section 9 with rasterio instead of GDAL in the threads. Explain the difference.
Using the illustrative prices, at how many runs per month does buying a GPU workstation pay off?

References

Rocklin, M. (2015). Dask: Parallel computation with blocked algorithms and task scheduling. Proc. 14th Python in Science Conference, 130-136.
Hoyer, S. & Hamman, J. (2017). xarray: N-D labeled arrays and datasets in Python. Journal of Open Research Software, 5(1).
Abernathey, R. P. et al. (2021). Cloud-native repositories for big scientific data. Computing in Science & Engineering, 23(2), 26-35.
Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall’s tau. JASA, 63, 1379-1389.
Okuta, R. et al. (2017). CuPy: A NumPy-compatible library for NVIDIA GPU calculations. Proc. LearningSys, NIPS.
Amdahl, G. M. (1967). Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities. AFIPS Conference Proceedings, 30, 483-485.

"""Pure functions that turn one day's Sentinel-2 bands into statistics. No input/output: easy to test."""

from __future__ import annotations

import math

import numpy as np

CLEAR_CLASSES = (4, 5, 6)  # SCL: vegetation, bare soil, water
EXPECTED = {"clear_fraction": (0.0, 1.0), "water_fraction": (0.0, 1.0), "ndvi_land_median": (-1.0, 1.0)}


def reflectance(dn: np.ndarray, processing_baseline: str | float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Surface reflectance from Sentinel-2 L2A DN as distributed by ESA / Planetary Computer.

    From processing baseline 04.00 (January 2022) DN carry an offset of 1000:
    reflectance = (DN - 1000) / 10000. Earlier baselines have no offset. DN 0 means no data.
    """
    offset = 1000.0 if float(processing_baseline) >= 4.0 else 0.0
    out = (dn.astype("float32") - offset) / 10_000.0
    out[dn == 0] = np.nan
    return out


def scene_stats(green: np.ndarray, red: np.ndarray, nir: np.ndarray, scl: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    """Clear fraction, open-water fraction (NDWI > 0) and median land NDVI of one observation.

    Bands are reflectances on the same grid; ``scl`` is the scene classification layer.
    """
    clear = np.isin(scl, CLEAR_CLASSES) & np.isfinite(green) & np.isfinite(red) & np.isfinite(nir)
    n = int(scl.size)
    if not clear.any():
        return {"pixels": n, "clear_fraction": 0.0, "water_fraction": math.nan, "ndvi_land_median": math.nan}
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        ndwi = (green - nir) / (green + nir)
        ndvi = (nir - red) / (nir + red)
    water = clear & (ndwi > 0)
    land = clear & ~water
    return {
        "pixels": n,
        "clear_fraction": float(clear.mean()),
        "water_fraction": float(water.sum() / clear.sum()),
        "ndvi_land_median": float(np.nanmedian(ndvi[land])) if land.any() else math.nan,
    }


def quality_flags(stats: dict, min_clear: float = 0.2) -> list[str]:
    """Data-quality checks; an empty list means the observation is usable."""
    flags = []
    for key, (lo, hi) in EXPECTED.items():
        value = stats.get(key)
        if value is None:
            flags.append(f"missing:{key}")
        elif not math.isnan(value) and not lo <= value <= hi:
            flags.append(f"out_of_range:{key}")
    if stats.get("clear_fraction", 0.0) < min_clear:
        flags.append("low_clear_fraction")
    return flags



process.py holds the science: the reflectance offset of Notebook 08_09 (which depends on the processing baseline), the cloud mask (scene classes vegetation, bare soil and water count as clear), open water as NDWI > 0, and data-quality flags. It has no input/output, so it is tested with small synthetic arrays. stac.py searches the catalogue and reads bands; pipeline.py combines them, skips dates already processed, writes the table atomically and logs every step as JSON.


Code
# Show the pipeline entry points used by CLI, CI, and the schedule
display(Code(filename=str(PROJECT / "src/haor_monitor/pipeline.py"), language="python"))


"""The monitoring job: find new observations, process them, append to the table, log the run.

Idempotent: dates already in ``observations.parquet`` are skipped, so the job can run on any
schedule, be retried after a failure, or run twice by accident without duplicating data.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import logging
import time
import uuid
from datetime import date, datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from . import stac
from .config import Settings
from .process import quality_flags, scene_stats

log = logging.getLogger("haor_monitor")
COLUMNS = [
    "date",
    "scenes",
    "baseline",
    "pixels",
    "clear_fraction",
    "water_fraction",
    "ndvi_land_median",
    "flags",
    "processed_at",
]


class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    """One JSON object per log line: easy to search and aggregate in any log service."""

    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        entry = {
            "time": datetime.fromtimestamp(record.created, timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "message": record.getMessage(),
        }
        entry.update(getattr(record, "fields", {}))
        return json.dumps(entry)


def setup_logging(path: Path | None = None) -> None:
    handlers: list[logging.Handler] = [logging.StreamHandler()]
    if path is not None:
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        handlers.append(logging.FileHandler(path))
    for handler in handlers:
        handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())
    log.handlers[:] = handlers
    log.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    log.propagate = False


def table_path(settings: Settings) -> Path:
    return settings.data_dir / "observations.parquet"


def load_table(settings: Settings) -> pd.DataFrame:
    path = table_path(settings)
    if path.exists():
        return pd.read_parquet(path)
    return pd.DataFrame(columns=COLUMNS)


def run(settings: Settings, start: date, end: date, *, search=stac.search, load=stac.load_day) -> dict:
    """Process every new daily observation between start and end; return a run summary."""
    run_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    settings.data_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    table = load_table(settings)
    done = set(pd.to_datetime(table["date"]).dt.date) if len(table) else set()
    days = stac.group_by_day(search(settings, start, end))
    new = {d: items for d, items in days.items() if d not in done}
    log.info(
        "run started",
        extra={
            "fields": {
                "run_id": run_id,
                "start": str(start),
                "end": str(end),
                "days_found": len(days),
                "days_new": len(new),
            }
        },
    )
    rows, failed = [], []
    for day, items in new.items():
        try:
            bands = load(items, settings)
            stats = scene_stats(bands["green"], bands["red"], bands["nir"], bands["scl"])
            flags = quality_flags(stats, settings.min_clear)
            rows.append(
                {
                    "date": pd.Timestamp(day),
                    "scenes": len(items),
                    "baseline": bands["baseline"],
                    **stats,
                    "flags": ";".join(flags),
                    "processed_at": pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC"),
                }
            )
            log.info(
                "day processed",
                extra={"fields": {"run_id": run_id, "date": str(day), **stats, "flags": flags}},
            )
        except Exception as exc:  # one bad day must not stop the run
            failed.append(str(day))
            log.error(
                "day failed",
                extra={
                    "fields": {"run_id": run_id, "date": str(day), "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"}
                },
            )
    if rows:
        new_rows = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=COLUMNS)
        table = new_rows if table.empty else pd.concat([table, new_rows], ignore_index=True)
        table = table.sort_values("date").reset_index(drop=True)
        tmp = table_path(settings).with_suffix(".tmp")
        table.to_parquet(tmp, index=False)
        tmp.replace(table_path(settings))  # atomic: readers never see a half-written file
    summary = {
        "run_id": run_id,
        "days_found": len(days),
        "days_new": len(new),
        "processed": len(rows),
        "failed": failed,
        "rows_total": len(table),
        "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1),
    }
    log.info("run finished", extra={"fields": summary})
    return summary

FAILED tests/test_process.py::test_reflectance_offset_depends_on_processing_baseline


The test suite failed (exit code 1, after 1.3 s) at test_reflectance_offset_depends_on_processing_baseline. For a pre-2022 scene (baseline 03.01), DN 1000 and 1500 now give reflectances of 0.0 and 0.05 instead of 0.10 and 0.15. Every older scene would silently become 0.1 darker, and NDVI and water fractions would shift with it.
On GitHub this pull request would show a red check and could not be merged under branch protection. The test exists because Notebook 08_09 found exactly this kind of offset confusion between data providers.

title: DevOps for Geospatial Pipelines: Packaging, Testing, CI, Containers and Schedules
section: Version control and the CI workflow
text:
Version control and the CI workflow
The project becomes a git repository (here a copy under the outputs folder, so the tutorial folder stays untouched). .gitignore keeps data and caches out of the code history.


Code
# Copy the project into the output folder and make an initial git commit
repo = OUT / "haor_monitor"
shutil.copytree(PROJECT, repo, ignore=shutil.ignore_patterns("__pycache__", ".pytest_cache", ".ruff_cache", ".coverage"))
(repo / ".gitignore").write_text("monitor_data/\n__pycache__/\n.pytest_cache/\n.ruff_cache/\n.coverage\n*.egg-info/\n")
for cmd in [["init", "-q"], ["add", "."], ["commit", "-q", "-m", "haor_monitor 1.0.0: pipeline, tests, Dockerfile, workflows"]]:
    assert sh(GIT + cmd, cwd=repo)[0] == 0
print(sh(["git", "log", "--stat", "--format=%h %s"], cwd=repo)[2])

The CI workflow is a YAML file. Each job runs on a fresh virtual machine; strategy.matrix repeats the job for three Python versions. Below we read the workflow and run its run: steps locally, in the committed copy, skipping the install step (the environment already has the packages) and the Docker job (Section 7).


Code
# Inspect the CI workflow, then replay its runnable steps locally
display(Code(filename=str(repo / ".github/workflows/ci.yml"), language="yaml"))
wf = yaml.safe_load((repo / ".github/workflows/ci.yml").read_text())
triggers = wf[True] if True in wf else wf["on"]                      # YAML 1.1 reads the key `on` as True
print("triggers:", list(triggers), "| jobs:", list(wf["jobs"]), "| Python versions:", wf["jobs"]["test"]["strategy"]["matrix"]["python-version"])
rows = []
for step in wf["jobs"]["test"]["steps"]:
    if "run" not in step:
        rows.append({"step": step.get("uses"), "result": "action (runs on GitHub)"}); continue
    if step["run"].startswith("pip install"):
        rows.append({"step": step["name"], "result": "skipped here (environment ready)"}); continue
    # Map workflow shell lines onto the local Python interpreter
    cmd = step["run"].replace("pytest", f"{PY} -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider").replace("ruff", f"{PY} -m ruff").split()
    code_, sec, out = sh(cmd, cwd=repo, env={"PYTHONPATH": f"{repo / 'src'}:{repo}"})
    rows.append({"step": step["name"], "command": step["run"], "result": "pass" if code_ == 0 else f"FAIL ({code_})",
                 "seconds": round(sec, 1)})
(repo / ".coverage").unlink(missing_ok=True)
pd.DataFrame(rows)


# Continuous integration: lint and test on every push and pull request.
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: pip
      - name: Install
        run: pip install -e ".[dev]"
      - name: Lint
        run: ruff check .
      - name: Format check
        run: ruff format --check .
      - name: Test
        run: pytest --cov=haor_monitor --cov-report=term-missing --cov-fail-under=80

  image:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build the container image
        run: docker build -t haor-monitor:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Smoke test the image
        run: docker run --rm haor-monitor:${{ github.sha }} report

The workflow runs on pushes to main and on pull requests, with two jobs:

test: lint, format check and tests with coverage, repeated for Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12.
image: runs only if the tests pass; builds the Docker image and smoke-tests it.

Run locally, its three check steps passed in the committed copy. Checkout, Python setup and installation are done by GitHub’s runners, and the image job needs Docker (Section 7). The first commit records the 17 files of version 1.0.0; the generated .gitignore keeps data and caches out of the code history.

title: DevOps for Geospatial Pipelines: Packaging, Testing, CI, Containers and Schedules
text:
Containers
A container image bundles the code with an operating system layer and every dependency, so the pipeline runs identically on a laptop, in CI, on a VM or in a managed service (AWS Batch, Cloud Run jobs, Azure Container Apps jobs, Kubernetes CronJobs).


Code
# Review the Dockerfile and check common container hardening practices
display(Code(filename=str(PROJECT / "Dockerfile"), language="docker"))
dockerfile = (PROJECT / "Dockerfile").read_text()
ignore = (PROJECT / ".dockerignore").read_text().split()
checks = {
    "base image pinned to an exact version": bool(re.search(r"^FROM \S+:\d+\.\d+\.\d+", dockerfile, re.M)),
    "slim base image": "slim" in dockerfile,
    "runs as a non-root user": bool(re.search(r"^USER (?!root)\S+", dockerfile, re.M)),
    "no secrets in ENV (KEY, TOKEN, PASSWORD, SECRET)": not re.search(r"^ENV .*(KEY|TOKEN|PASSWORD|SECRET)", dockerfile, re.M | re.I),
    "pip cache disabled (smaller image)": "PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1" in dockerfile,
    "data mounted as a volume, not baked in": "VOLUME" in dockerfile and "monitor_data/" in ignore,
    "tests and git history excluded from the build context": "tests/" in ignore and ".git/" in ignore,
    "no ADD of remote URLs": not re.search(r"^ADD https?://", dockerfile, re.M),
}
display(pd.Series(checks, name="passes").to_frame())

# Build and smoke-test the image when Docker is available
if shutil.which("docker"):
    code_, sec, out = sh(["docker", "build", "-t", "haor-monitor:1.0.0", "."], cwd=repo)
    print(f"docker build: exit {code_} in {sec:.0f} s")
    code_, sec, out = sh(["docker", "run", "--rm", "haor-monitor:1.0.0", "report"], cwd=repo)
    print("docker run report:", out.splitlines()[-1] if out else code_)
else:
    print("Docker is not installed on this machine: the image is built by the `image` job of the CI workflow instead.")


# Container image for the Tanguar Haor monitor (GeoLattice Notebook 08_10).
#   docker build -t haor-monitor:1.0.0 .
#   docker run --rm -v "$PWD/monitor_data:/data" haor-monitor:1.0.0 run --start 2024-01-01 --end 2024-12-31
FROM python:3.11.11-slim-bookworm

ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
    HAOR_DATA_DIR=/data

# rasterio and odc-stac install from wheels that bundle GDAL: no system GDAL needed
WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml README.md ./
COPY src ./src
RUN pip install . && useradd --create-home --uid 10001 monitor && mkdir /data && chown monitor /data

USER monitor
VOLUME ["/data"]
HEALTHCHECK NONE
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-m", "haor_monitor"]
CMD ["run"]

The Dockerfile passes all eight checks:

an exact, slim base image (python:3.11.11-slim-bookworm);
a non-root user;
no secrets in environment variables;
no pip cache;
data on a volume rather than in the image;
tests and git history excluded from the build context;
no downloads with ADD.

rasterio and odc-stac install from wheels that bundle GDAL, so no system GDAL packages are needed.
Docker is not installed on this machine, so the image was not built here. The image job of the CI workflow builds it on every change instead. On a machine with Docker, the same cell builds the image and runs report inside it. Use hadolint for a complete lint of Dockerfiles.

title: DevOps for Geospatial Pipelines: Packaging, Testing, CI, Containers and Schedules
text:
Scheduled, idempotent runs
monitor.yml runs the pipeline on a cron schedule (30 6 */5 * *: 06:30 UTC every fifth day, matching Sentinel-2’s revisit), never two runs at once (concurrency), and commits the results to a data branch.


Code
# Inspect the scheduled monitoring workflow (cron, concurrency, timeout)
display(Code(filename=str(repo / ".github/workflows/monitor.yml"), language="yaml"))
mon = yaml.safe_load((repo / ".github/workflows/monitor.yml").read_text())
mon_on = mon[True] if True in mon else mon["on"]
print("schedule:", mon_on["schedule"][0]["cron"], "| concurrency:", mon["concurrency"], "| timeout:", mon["jobs"]["run"]["timeout-minutes"], "min")


# Scheduled monitoring: every 5 days (Sentinel-2's revisit), plus manual runs.
# Results are kept on the `data` branch, so every update is versioned by git.
name: monitor

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "30 6 */5 * *"          # 06:30 UTC every fifth day of the month
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      start:
        description: "First date (YYYY-MM-DD); default: 30 days ago"
        required: false

concurrency:
  group: monitor                     # never two runs at once: they would race on the table
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: data
          path: monitor_data
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: pip
      - name: Install
        run: pip install .
      - name: Run the monitor
        env:
          HAOR_DATA_DIR: monitor_data
        run: python -m haor_monitor run ${{ inputs.start && format('--start {0}', inputs.start) || '' }}
      - name: Commit new observations
        working-directory: monitor_data
        run: |
          git config user.name "haor-monitor bot"
          git config user.email "actions@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add observations.parquet runs.jsonl
          git diff --cached --quiet || git commit -m "Observations update $(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)"
          git push



schedule: 30 6 */5 * * | concurrency: {'group': 'monitor', 'cancel-in-progress': False} | timeout: 60 min


We imitate three scheduled runs against the real catalogue. The data folder is its own git repository, standing in for the data branch, and each run’s results are committed when they changed:

a first run covering January to June 2024;
the same window again, as when a scheduler fires twice or a run is retried;
a later run covering the whole year, after the second half of 2024 “arrived”.



Code
# Run the monitor CLI for a few date windows and commit data changes
data_dir = OUT / "monitor_data"
data_dir.mkdir()
assert sh(GIT + ["init", "-q"], cwd=data_dir)[0] == 0
runs = []
for start, end in [("2024-01-01", "2024-06-30"), ("2024-01-01", "2024-06-30"), ("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31")]:
    code_, sec, out = sh([PY, "-m", "haor_monitor", "run", "--start", start, "--end", end], cwd=repo,
                         env={"PYTHONPATH": str(repo / "src"), "HAOR_DATA_DIR": str(data_dir)})
    summary = [json.loads(l) for l in out.splitlines() if l.startswith("{") and '"run finished"' in l][-1]
    sh(GIT + ["add", "-A"], cwd=data_dir)
    committed = sh(GIT + ["commit", "-q", "-m", f"observations {start} to {end}"], cwd=data_dir)[0] == 0
    runs.append({"window": f"{start} to {end}", "exit code": code_, "days found": summary["days_found"],
                 "new": summary["days_new"], "processed": summary["processed"], "failed": len(summary["failed"]),
                 "rows in table": summary["rows_total"], "seconds": round(sec, 1), "data commit": committed})

The data quality flags removed one observation, 2 September 2024, when the haor was completely cloud-covered.
The 30 usable observations trace the haor’s year:

Dry season: open water fell from 31% of the clear area on 1 January to 3.6% at the end of January.
Boro rice: land NDVI peaked at 0.70 in mid-March.
Monsoon gap: there is no usable optical observation from June to August.
Flood: after the monsoon the haor was 97.7% water on 17 October, then drained to 47% by 31 December.

The monsoon gap is the limit of optical monitoring here. Notebook 08_11 fills it with Sentinel-1 radar, which sees through cloud.

title: DevOps for Geospatial Pipelines: Packaging, Testing, CI, Containers and Schedules
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Put science in pure functions, input/output at the edges, and configuration in the environment.
Tests that need no network run in seconds anywhere; quality gates make style and coverage automatic.
CI runs the same checks on every change on a clean machine; a red build blocks a bad merge.
Containers fix the environment; keep images small, pinned and non-root, and keep data and secrets out.
Scheduled jobs must be idempotent (safe to repeat), observable (structured logs, exit codes) and write atomically; version their outputs.

What we did

The project: a package (342 lines), tests (190 lines), a Dockerfile and two workflows.
Quality gates: lint, format and 12 tests with 93% coverage, all passing; a deliberately broken offset rule was caught by a test in 1.3 s.
Git and CI: git history for code and data; the CI workflow’s checks run locally, green.
Container: the Dockerfile passes 8 best-practice checks. It is built by CI; Docker is not available here.
Scheduled runs: three simulated runs against Planetary Computer (16, 0 and 15 new days) gave a 31-row table without duplicates, logged as JSON lines.
Science: Tanguar Haor was 97.7% open water in October 2024 and 3.6% in January; Boro rice NDVI peaked at 0.70 in March.

Exercises

Add a test that fails if a day’s water_fraction changes by more than 0.5 between consecutive usable observations, and decide whether that is a data error or a real event.
Add HAOR_RESOLUTION=10 support to the CI matrix as a second configuration. What does it cost in run time?
Make the pipeline write a small STAC catalogue (one item per observation) next to the table.
Replace the GitHub Actions schedule with a Kubernetes CronJob manifest that runs the container image.
Send an alert (an issue, an email or a chat message) when the monitor workflow fails, using the job’s failure status.

References

Kim, G., Humble, J., Debois, P. & Willis, J. (2021). The DevOps Handbook, 2nd ed. IT Revolution.
GitHub Actions documentation. https://docs.github.com/actions
Docker best practices for building images. https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/
pytest and ruff documentation. https://docs.pytest.org, https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/
Ramsar Sites Information Service: Tanguar Haor (site no. 1031). https://rsis.ramsar.org
